findings.title: LiteralValue equality ignores DateTimeOffset offset and decimal scale, but the printers keep both
findings.summary: Equals and GetHashCode compare decimals with == (1.0m == 1.00m) and DateTimeOffsets with == (instant only, offset ignored). ToString (line 349, 351), and so TermIdentity.ToString, CanonicalPrinter (CanonicalPrinter.cs:177) and TreeFormatEmitter, keep the scale and the offset. Two terms are one TermIdentity (one memo key, one analyzer variable) while their canonical text and the PredicateArguments the predicate reads are different. CONTEXT.md 'Term identity' says arguments compare by 'exact type-normalized value', and ADR-0003 says canonical printed forms can be compared directly.
findings.failure_scenario: Take `p(at: "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z") AND p(at: "2024-01-01T02:00:00+02:00")`, where p is a custom predicate that reads args.GetDateTimeOffset("at").Offset or .Date (the calendar day in the written offset). The evaluator memoizes by TermIdentity, so p runs once and the second term silently reuses the first term's answer. A related case: `q(x: 1.0)` and `q(x: 1.00)` compile to equal Expression trees but give different CanonicalText, so a diff of canonical text reports a change where tree equality reports none.
findings.expected_behavior: Identity equality and canonical text agree. Either normalize at construction (decimal scale, a fixed offset or UTC) or include the scale and offset in Equals and GetHashCode.

findings.title: OperatorInfo.Describe returns label 'Forall'/'Exists' with an empty description for a quantifier
findings.summary: ExpressionShape.Of gives a QuantifierExpression the op-name 'Forall' or 'Exists' (NodeShape.cs:67). OperatorDefinitions has no entry for either, so the public OperatorInfo.Describe falls through to `new OperatorDescriptor(shape.OpName, string.Empty)`. Every other surface writes FORALL/EXISTS (QuantifierText.Label, the docs/strong-k3/quantifiers trace labels). ADR-0005 decision 18 counts the quantifiers as connectives, and the XML doc says every operator has a descriptor.
findings.failure_scenario: A library consumer calls OperatorInfo.Describe(new QuantifierExpression(QuantifierKind.ForAll, "line", "lines", body)) to build a UI label. The call returns Label="Forall" and Description="", which disagrees with the outline and trace label FORALL and leaves the description empty. The internal outline code avoids this only because it special-cases quantifiers first (CompiledRule.Printing.cs:657-676).
findings.expected_behavior: Describe returns QuantifierText.Label(kind) and a real description for a quantifier, or the API documents that a quantifier is rejected the way a TermExpression is.

findings.title: Tree-format 'did you mean' candidates leave out forall/exists
findings.summary: ReadableNames is documented as every op string a tree may use when reading, and TreeFormatReader uses it as the suggestion candidates (TreeFormatReader.cs:399). The table is built only from OperatorDefinitions plus xnor/iff (lines 50-60), so 'forall' and 'exists' are missing. Those two ops are read by a special case before this lookup (TreeFormatReader.cs:379-387).
findings.failure_scenario: JSON `{"op": "foral", "var": "line", "in": "lines", "operands": [...]}` gives 'Unknown operator' with no suggestion. No remaining candidate is within the 2-edit cut-off for a 5-character word, so the author is not told about 'forall'. A typo of any other op gets a suggestion.
findings.expected_behavior: ReadableNames includes forall and exists, so a quantifier typo gets the same 'did you mean' as every other op.

findings.title: ADR-0005 still says Decision.Project(bool); the docs and code use Project(TruthValue) and reject Unknown at run time
findings.summary: ADR-0005 decision 12 (line 335) and decision 19 (line 625) say the method is `Decision.Project(bool unknownAs)`, with a bool 'so an Unknown replacement cannot be requested'. The code, docs/strong-k3/result-transformations/project.md and CONTEXT.md all use Project(TruthValue) and throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException for Unknown. The docs and code agree, so the ADR is the stale side: it records a compile-time guarantee that no longer exists, and no amendment records the change.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader who trusts the ADR expects decision.Project(TruthValue.Unknown) not to compile. It compiles and throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException at run time.
findings.expected_behavior: ADR-0005 gets an amendment that records the TruthValue parameter and the run-time check, so the ADR matches project.md.

findings.title: EQUIVALENT description calls XNOR 'formerly', but XNOR is a current alias
findings.summary: The description that OperatorInfo returns publicly reads 'Logical biconditional (IFF, formerly XNOR) ...'. docs/strong-k3/specification/operations.md lists 'Aliases IFF and XNOR', and the DSL and tree formats still accept XNOR. The documentation standard says reference text describes current behavior, not history.
findings.failure_scenario: A rule-authoring UI shows the description for an EQUIVALENT node, and a reader concludes that XNOR is no longer accepted, which is wrong.
findings.expected_behavior: The description names IFF and XNOR as aliases, with no 'formerly'.

findings.title: TruthValueText cites the wrong ADR-0005 decision
findings.summary: The summary says the spelling table implements 'ADR-0005 decision 11'. Decision 11 covers structured validation messages. The constant spellings (case-insensitive True/False/Unknown, JSON 'unknown', the T/F/U letters) are decision 16.
findings.failure_scenario: A maintainer follows the reference to check how the letters or the JSON 'unknown' constant should be read and lands on the diagnostics decision instead.
findings.expected_behavior: The comment cites ADR-0005 decision 16.

reviewers.label: F2 Parsing
reviewers.coverage:
I read all of DslParser.cs, Lexer.cs, TreeFormatReader.cs, RuleNode.cs, NoteAttacher.cs, Token.cs, DslVocabulary.cs, ReservedWords.cs, RawLiteral.cs (lines 40-78), TreePath.cs and TreePathTracker.cs. I did not open CollapseRejection.cs, NxorRejection.cs, ProjectRejection.cs, Comment.cs, NoteText.cs, ITreeNodeCursor.cs, TreeFormatVocabulary.cs, TreeMember.cs or VariableParts.cs. They are small helpers, and I only saw them through their call sites.

Outside the slice, I read what I needed to place the limits: OperatorDefinitions.cs (symbol table), RuleCompiler.cs, RuleNodeCompiler.cs (40-270 and 708-760), DefinitionExpander.cs (20-130 and 210-302), JsonTreeParser.cs, JsonNodeCursor.cs, YamlNodeCursor.cs (58-215), YamlTreeParser.cs (20-80) and LiteralConversion.cs (20-95). For docs, I read docs/strong-k3/specification/syntax.md, notation.md, docs/rule-text.md lines 1-170 and ADR-0008 in full. ADR-0005 and ADR-0006 I only reached through grep and code references, not a full read.

Every symbol alias the lexer emits matches OperatorDefinitions.ReadSymbols. I traced NOT > AND > OR precedence, every row of the mixing-rule table in syntax.md, the ternary rules, IFF/XNOR aliasing and the T/F/U-followed-by-( rule, and they all match the docs.

Three findings have parts outside the slice and are flagged as such: the exponential definition expansion is in DefinitionExpander, the JSON depth cap is in JsonTreeParser, and the duplicate-key handling sits in the JSON cursor and parser, even though TreeFormatReader.CheckKeys anchors the finding.

The Lexer recursion on invalid characters depends on whether the JIT turns `return this.NextToken()` into a tail call. I did not confirm that, which is why it is folded into the stack-depth finding and not reported on its own.

Not reviewed: printers and how they round-trip, the RuleBuilder JSON path, the RuleDefinitions reader, and the tests (I used them only to confirm that no deep-nesting parse test exists).

findings.title: DSL definition parameter named T/F/U/True/False/Unknown is silently read as a constant (JSON reads it as the parameter)
findings.summary: ParsePrimary checks the constant keywords (TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN at 552-565, T/F/U at 569-585) before it checks the current definition's parameters (688-698). ExpectParameterName (799) accepts any identifier, and DefinitionExpander does not check parameter names: it has no reserved-word or unused-parameter check. So a parameter called t, f, u, true, false or unknown is never referenced, and its argument is silently dropped. TreeFormatReader (237-247) reads the same definition as a ParameterReferenceNode, so the DSL and JSON/YAML give different trees for the same document. rule-text.md:80-81 says each parameter can be used 'wherever a term, constant or sub-expression could appear'.
findings.failure_scenario: `let gate(t) = t AND isAdult; gate(isBanned)` compiles with no diagnostic to `True AND isAdult`, so a banned adult gets True. The JSON form `{"definitions":{"gate":{"parameters":["t"],"body":{"op":"and","operands":[{"predicate":"t"},{"predicate":"isAdult"}]}}},"op":"use","name":"gate","operands":[{"predicate":"isBanned"}]}` compiles to `isBanned AND isAdult`. The code looks wrong here: either reject reserved parameter names as DefinitionNameCollision, or check parameters before the constants.
findings.expected_behavior: A parameter name that is a reserved word or T/F/U is a compile error, or the parameter always wins inside the body, the same in every format.
findings.evidence:
I traced `let gate(t) = t AND isAdult; gate(isBanned)` through the code.

1. `ParseDefinition` (DslParser.cs:761-797) reads parameters with `ExpectParameterName` (799-804). That method only requires an Identifier token. It does no reserved-word, T/F/U or duplicate check. The parameter set is stored in `currentParameters` (790).
2. While parsing the body, `ParsePrimary` reaches the bare identifier `t`. It is not followed by `(`, so the T/F/U branch at 569-575 matches first (`IsKeyword("T")`, which is case-insensitive) and returns `ConsumeConstant(True)`.
3. The parameter-reference branch (688-698) comes later, so it is never reached. The same ordering applies to TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN at 552-565, which are also checked before the parameter branch.
4. `DefinitionExpander.ExpandUse` (292-299) binds `t` to the argument, but the body holds no `ParameterReferenceNode`, so the argument is dropped. The only checks are argument count (262), cycles, depth, and definition-name reserved words (line 45 checks `definition.Name` only). No parameter names are validated, and the arity check passes. The result is `True AND isAdult` with no diagnostic.
5. TreeFormatReader (237-247) reads the same definition as a `ParameterReferenceNode`, so JSON/YAML give `isBanned AND isAdult`. The DSL and JSON therefore differ for the same document.

The failure needs a parameter named t, f, u, true, false or unknown. A single letter like `t` is a plausible name, so the trigger is realistic. The result is a wrong authorization result with no diagnostic, so I rate it high rather than critical.

findings.title: Parsing recursion has no depth guard: deep nesting crashes the process with StackOverflowException before MaxDepth applies
findings.summary: MaxDepth is only enforced in RuleNodeCompiler.Build (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:226), after the full raw tree exists. The DSL parser recurses with no limit: about 9 frames per group level (ParsePrimary 538-548 -> ParseExpression -> ParseOrExpression -> ParseAndOrChain -> ... -> ParseNotExpression), and one frame per NOT (517-527, not a tail call because it builds the NotNode afterwards). NoteAttacher.Measure (NoteAttacher.cs:115) and TreeFormatReader.ReadNode/ReadOperator (149, 436) also recurse with no limit. The Lexer recurses once per invalid character (`return this.NextToken();`, Lexer.cs:132), so it depends on a JIT tail call, and it adds one diagnostic per character with no cap. A StackOverflowException cannot be caught, so this breaks 'Compile never throws' and kills the host.
findings.failure_scenario: `RuleCompiler.Compile(new string('(', 200_000) + "a" + new string(')', 200_000))`, or `string.Concat(Enumerable.Repeat("NOT ", 500_000)) + "a"`, terminates the process instead of returning TRE0009 MaxDepthExceeded. A deeply nested YAML document through CompileYaml, or a JsonElement parsed with a raised JsonDocumentOptions.MaxDepth through CompileJson(JsonElement), takes the same path through TreeFormatReader.
findings.expected_behavior: The parser and the tree reader stop at a nesting bound tied to CompilerOptions.MaxDepth (or call RuntimeHelpers.TryEnsureSufficientExecutionStack) and report a diagnostic.
findings.evidence: I traced the DSL parser path. I did not run it. A repo-wide grep of src/ for TryEnsureSufficientExecutionStack, EnsureSufficientExecutionStack, InsufficientExecutionStack, maxStackSize, new Thread, MaxLength, MaxSource and MaxInput found nothing. There is no stack guard and no input-size cap. In Parsing/DslParser.cs, the group case of ParsePrimary (lines 536-548) calls ParseExpression (281) -> ParseOrExpression (397) -> ParseAndOrChain (413) -> parseOperand delegate (ParseAndExpression 402) -> ParseAndOrChain -> ParseInfixChain -> ... -> ParseNotExpression -> ParsePrimary. Every '(' therefore adds a fixed stack of frames, and none of them checks depth. ParseNotExpression (517-527) calls itself once per NOT, then builds NotNode(operand, ...) afterward, so it is not a tail call. The only depth counters in Parsing/ are in a skip-ahead helper (lines 147-159) and a bracket-matching helper (379-388), and neither limits recursion. NoteAttacher.Measure (NoteAttacher.cs:117-133) recurses over operands with no guard. The MaxDepth check lives in RuleNodeCompiler.Build, which runs only after Parse has produced the whole tree. A StackOverflowException cannot be caught in .NET, so an input such as 200k '(' or 500k 'NOT ' kills the process before TRE0009 can be reported. I did not read the Lexer or TreeFormatReader lines the finding cites. The DSL parser path is enough to confirm the finding. Practical exposure is limited to untrusted rule text, since it takes a very large input (hundreds of thousands of nesting levels, or tens of thousands with the default 1 MB stack). It is still a denial-of-service against a host that compiles user-supplied rules. I assign medium-high severity, and I keep high because the failure is unrecoverable.

findings.title: JSON rules with duplicate keys are accepted last-wins, while YAML rejects the same document
findings.summary: JsonTreeParser parses with default JsonDocumentOptions (JsonTreeParser.cs:34), so duplicate properties are allowed. JsonNodeCursor.TryGetChild (JsonNodeCursor.cs:79) uses JsonElement.TryGetProperty, which returns the last duplicate. CheckKeys only checks each key name against the allowed list and does not detect repeats. Duplicate structural keys (`op`, `const`, `predicate`, `k`, `min`, `max`, `operands`, `note`, `name`, `var`, `in`) are therefore resolved silently by the last value. YamlDotNet rejects a repeated mapping key, so YAML gives an error (YamlTreeParser.cs:33-38). Only duplicate `args` names are caught, as TRE0032, because Members enumerates both. DecisionJsonReader already sets AllowDuplicateProperties = false.
findings.failure_scenario: `{"op":"and","op":"or","operands":[{"predicate":"isAdmin"},{"predicate":"isGuest"}]}` compiles as OR with no diagnostic. A reviewer or tool that reads the first key sees AND. The same document in YAML (`op: and` / `op: or`) is a compile error. `{"op":"atLeast","k":1,"k":3,...}` silently uses k = 3.
findings.expected_behavior: A repeated key in a rule tree node is MalformedTree (TRE0014) in JSON, as YAML already rejects it.
findings.evidence:
I traced the path in the code and did not run it. The finding's file paths are slightly off. The JSON files are in src/TruthWeaver/Json/, not Parsing/.

1. src/TruthWeaver/Json/JsonTreeParser.cs:34 calls `JsonDocument.Parse(json)` with default options. Duplicate properties are therefore allowed. DecisionJsonReader.cs:37 explicitly sets `AllowDuplicateProperties = false`, so the tree parser is inconsistent with it.
2. src/TruthWeaver/Json/JsonNodeCursor.cs:79 implements `TryGetChild` with `element.TryGetProperty(key, ...)`, which returns the last duplicate.
3. JsonNodeCursor.cs:145 implements `Members` with `EnumerateObject()`, which yields both duplicates. `CheckKeys` (src/TruthWeaver/Parsing/TreeFormatReader.cs:106-122) only tests each name against the allowed list with `allowed.Contains`. It never tracks repeated names. A repeated `op`, `k` or similar key is allowed and `TryGetChild` resolves it to the last value.
4. src/TruthWeaver/Json/JsonSpanLocator.cs:100 contains the comment "A repeated key keeps the last occurrence, the same one JsonElement.TryGetProperty resolves to". Last-wins is known, but I found no ADR or doc that makes it intended behavior. My doc grep found only YAML duplicate-key rejection documented, in docs/data-sources.md and the CHANGELOG.
5. src/TruthWeaver.Yaml/YamlTreeParser.cs:35 states that YamlDotNet rejects a repeated mapping key while loading. The same document therefore fails in YAML and compiles in JSON.

The claimed scenarios hold. `{"op":"and","op":"or",...}` compiles as OR with no diagnostic, and `"k":1,"k":3` silently uses 3.

Only `args` duplicates are reported (TRE0032, per the finding and RuleNodeCompiler.cs:753). I did not trace that path.

I lower the severity to medium. This is a correctness and consistency gap with a trivial fix (set `AllowDuplicateProperties = false`, or detect repeats in `CheckKeys`). It needs a deliberately ambiguous document. It could matter if the JSON is untrusted or reviewed by a tool that reads the first key, but it does not corrupt evaluation of well-formed rules.

findings.title: Definition expansion grows exponentially before MaxNodeCount is checked (tiny input exhausts memory)
findings.summary: ExpandUse expands the callee body again for every use and builds new nodes (ExpandNode/ExpandAll). The only bound during expansion is MaxDefinitionDepth (default 8), on chain length. MaxNodeCount is counted later in RuleNodeCompiler.Build, so the whole expanded raw tree is built first. ADR-0008 decision 6 says expanded nodes count toward MaxNodeCount, but nothing stops the expansion before it is materialized. This is outside the Parsing slice, but it is the same resource-limit gap.
findings.failure_scenario: Eight definitions, each the AND of 20 uses of the previous one (`let a1 = x AND x AND ... (20); let a2 = a1 AND a1 AND ... (20); ... let a8 = a7 AND ...; a8`). This is under 2 KB of text and asks for about 20^8 = 2.6e10 RawNode allocations, so Compile runs out of memory or runs for a very long time instead of returning TRE0010 MaxNodeCountExceeded.
findings.expected_behavior: The expander counts the nodes it produces and stops with MaxNodeCountExceeded when the count passes CompilerOptions.MaxNodeCount.
findings.evidence:
I traced the path in src/TruthWeaver/Compilation/DefinitionExpander.cs and found no node-count bound before expansion finishes.

- RuleNodeCompiler.cs:90 calls DefinitionExpander.Expand(document, registry, options) and gets the whole expanded raw tree back.
- RuleNodeCompiler.cs:206 is the only MaxNodeCount check. It runs afterwards, in the build pass.
- ExpandUse (DefinitionExpander.cs:298-299) calls ExpandNode(definition.Body, bound, nextChain, unused) on every use. ExpandNode rebuilds every body node through the Carry(..., new AndNode(ExpandAll(...))) arms at lines 133-182.
- Nothing caches or shares an expanded body between uses. Only argument nodes are shared, through the parameter dictionary at lines 292-296. The expander keeps no count of the nodes it creates.
- The only checks before a body is expanded are the cycle check, the argument-count check and chain.Count >= MaxDefinitionDepth (line 277). That last one limits chain length (default 8), not total size.

Trigger check: with a8 used at chain depth 0, a1 is used at chain depth 7, which is below 8, so the 8-level chain is allowed. Each level has 20 uses of the one below. That gives about 20^8 = 2.6e10 nodes, built from a parse tree of roughly 160 use nodes. I found no input-length or definition-count limit that would stop the text first.

Smaller cases are also a problem. A fan-out of 10 gives about 1e8 nodes, and a fan-out of 5 gives about 390,000. Both are far above the default MaxNodeCount of 512, so the caller expects a TRE0010 error. The documentation (CompilerOptions.cs:15 and ADR-0008) says expanded nodes count toward MaxNodeCount, but nothing enforces that during expansion, so the cap only works for small blow-ups.

I did not run the repro, so the memory-exhaustion claim rests on the traced allocation count, not on an observed crash. Compile does not return TRE0010 in this case. It allocates the full tree first, which is a denial-of-service on untrusted rule text.

findings.title: Comment-to-note attachment is quadratic and runs before any size limit
findings.summary: For each comment, FindTarget scans the token list from the start (67-83), then calls Deepest up to four times, and each call scans every extent with no early exit (95-107). The cost is O(comments x (tokens + nodes)). This runs inside DslParser.Parse (DslParser.cs:120), before MaxNodeCount or MaxDepth are checked.
findings.failure_scenario: About 1 MB of `a /**/ AND ` repeated gives about 90k comments, 180k tokens and 90k extents, so about 4e10 comparisons. Compile spends minutes of CPU before it reports TRE0010. A service that compiles user-written rules can be tied up this way.
findings.expected_behavior: Comments are attached in about linear time (for example, a binary search over sorted token offsets and extents indexed by start and end), or the parse stops at a size limit first.

findings.title: Duplicate definition parameter names are accepted; the last binding silently wins
findings.summary: ParseDefinition collects parameter names into a List with no uniqueness check (767-780). TreeFormatReader.ReadDefinitionEntry does the same (788-803). DefinitionExpander binds them into a case-insensitive dictionary by index (DefinitionExpander.cs:292-296), so a later duplicate overwrites an earlier one. The argument count still matches, so no diagnostic is raised and one argument is dropped. ADR-0008 decision 6 asks for argument-shape mistakes to be diagnostics, 'not silently absorbed'.
findings.failure_scenario: `let both(a, A) = a AND isAdult; both(isOwner, isEditor)` compiles to `isEditor AND isAdult`, and isOwner is ignored with no diagnostic. The JSON form with `"parameters":["a","A"]` gives the same result.
findings.expected_behavior: A repeated parameter name (compared without case) is a compile error, for example DefinitionNameCollision or a dedicated code.

findings.title: JSON depth cap (64) rejects rules that the DSL accepts under the same MaxDepth
findings.summary: CompileJson(string) uses JsonDocument.Parse with the default MaxDepth of 64. Each rule level takes two JSON levels (node object plus operands array). The JSON form therefore fails at about 31-32 rule levels, whatever CompilerOptions.MaxDepth is set to, and it fails as 'Malformed JSON' (TRE0014), not TRE0009. This breaks the cross-format and round-trip guarantee in rule-formats.md:16 when MaxDepth is raised.
findings.failure_scenario: With `new CompilerOptions(MaxDepth: 40)`, a 35-level NOT/AND chain compiles from rule text. Its PrintJson() output fed to CompileJson fails with 'Malformed JSON: The maximum configured depth of 64 has been exceeded'. At the default MaxDepth of 32, a 32-level rule whose deepest term has an array argument also goes past the JSON depth.
findings.expected_behavior: The JSON reader's MaxDepth comes from CompilerOptions.MaxDepth (about 2 x MaxDepth plus room for argument values), so the depth limit trips the same way in every format.

findings.title: Error recovery cascades into misleading follow-on diagnostics
findings.summary: When ParsePrimary meets an unexpected token, it always consumes it (720-723), even when the token is a closer that an enclosing group is waiting for. ParseIntegerBound only skips a NumberLiteral (1148-1151), so a missing k leaves the operand in place, and then ExpectClose and the top level report it again.
findings.failure_scenario: `(a AND )` reports 'Expected a term...' and then a false 'Unclosed '(' ... expected ')' before the end of the rule', though the paren is closed. `AtLeast(a, b, c)` (k forgotten) gives three errors: InvalidThresholdValue at a, "Expected ')' ... found 'a'", and "Unexpected token 'a' after end of expression".
findings.expected_behavior: Do not consume a closer that matches an open group. After a bad bound, skip to the next ',' or ')' so that one mistake gives one diagnostic.

findings.title: Reserved operator words in operand position parse as terms, giving 'reserved predicate name' instead of a syntax error
findings.summary: Any identifier that does not match a primary keyword falls into ParseTerm. That includes infix words (AND, OR, XOR, IMPLIES, NAND, NOR, EQUIVALENT, IFF, XNOR). The mistake is then reported by the compiler as UnknownPredicate "'OR' is a reserved word and cannot be a predicate name". syntax.md:48 says `AND(a, b)` and `XOR(a, b)` are syntax errors.
findings.failure_scenario: `a AND OR` (missing operand) and `XOR()` or `XOR(x: 1)` give UnknownPredicate (reserved word) and no SyntaxError, so the message points the author at predicate naming instead of the missing operand or the call form that is not allowed.
findings.expected_behavior: An infix operator word in operand position is a SyntaxError ('expected a term, constant or (') at that token.

findings.title: TreePath bracket form does not escape backslash, so two different keys can share one path
findings.summary: Property escapes a single quote as \' but leaves a backslash as it is. The key a' and the key a\ both become $['a\']. A path no longer identifies one node, and diagnostics, JsonSpanLocator and CompiledRule.Notes are keyed by path.
findings.failure_scenario: A JSON definitions section with entries named "a'" and "a\\" (or predicate args with those names) gives both diagnostics the path $.definitions['a\'], so the span locator can underline the wrong entry.
findings.expected_behavior: Escape the backslash before the quote, so each key has its own path.

findings.title: Rule-text grammar omits the from(...) variable-reference argument value
findings.summary: The EBNF gives `argument = identifier ":" literal` and lists literals as string, number, true, false or an array. The parser also accepts `from("source", "query")` as a whole argument value (DslParser.cs:843, 851-881, ADR-0006 decision 10). The grammar in the docs is incomplete. Here the doc is the side that is wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: An author or tool writer who follows the published grammar treats `limit: from("limits", "$.max")` as invalid, though the engine accepts it. They also cannot tell from the grammar that from(...) is not allowed inside an array.
findings.expected_behavior: Add `argument = identifier ":" ( literal | variable )` and `variable = "from" "(" string "," string ")"` to the grammar.

reviewers.label: F3 Compilation
reviewers.coverage: Fully read: src/TruthWeaver/Compilation/RuleNodeCompiler.cs, RuleCompiler.cs, DefinitionExpander.cs, RuleDefinitions.cs, CompilerOptions.cs, NoteCollector.cs, LiteralConversion.cs, DataSourceDeclarations.cs, CompilationResult.cs and LintRules.cs. Read as context: ADR-0008 in full, the ADR-0010 node-count clause, docs/strong-k3/cardinality k/min/max range text (the code's ValidThresholdRange and BETWEEN bounds match the docs), docs/rule-text.md definitions section, docs/tool-core.md Lenient section, OperatorDefinitions.cs (the arity table matches the RuleNodeCompiler checks for every operator: NOT 1, binary 2..2, the variadics >=2, the thresholds >=1, BETWEEN >=2, If 3, inspections 1), CollectionBinding.CompileBody, the PredicateSchema.ArgumentValidator contract (must not throw, so I did not report validator exceptions), and relevant DslParser/TreeFormatReader snippets. Not read: CompilationMode.cs, DefinitionDeclaration.cs, DefinitionUse.cs, FailedNode.cs and RuleFormat.cs (each 18-35 lines of declarations), and ADR-0001/0002/0005/0006 in full (I checked only the sections my findings depend on). Arity and threshold/BETWEEN validation, the per-predicate argument checks (duplicate, unknown, missing, kind, default, deprecation, data-source and query checks) and the early return on front-end errors in the Parse-Validate-Analyze-Build flow all matched the docs. The one throw path in this slice (ArityOf/ValidThresholdRange/unhandled node) is reachable only through programming errors.

findings.title: let expansion has no size budget: a short document hangs or exhausts memory in Compile (and in RuleDefinitions.ReadText)
findings.summary: DefinitionExpander expands every use eagerly and allocates a fresh copy of each definition body (ExpandUse -> ExpandNode at 298-299, new nodes via Carry/ExpandAll) without counting nodes. MaxNodeCount is enforced only afterwards, in RuleNodeCompiler.Build (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:90-95), and MaxDefinitionDepth (8) bounds chain length, not fan-out. So the expanded size is fanout^depth before any limit runs. RuleDefinitions.Reader.Expand (RuleDefinitions.cs:263-332) walks the same expansion with no budget and records a path string per expanded node, so the public RuleDefinitions.ReadText, which needs no registry, has the same blowup. This breaks the CompilerOptions promise (CompilerOptions.cs:4-5) that rule text from an unreviewed source cannot hang a request thread, and ADR-0008 decision 6's claim that MaxDefinitionDepth catches a runaway chain 'long before it could threaten MaxNodeCount'.
findings.failure_scenario: Rule text (about 1.5 KB): `let d0 = p; let d1 = d0 AND d0 AND ... (20 times); let d2 = d1 AND ... (20 times); ... let d7 = d6 AND ... (20 times); d7`. The chain depth is 7, below MaxDefinitionDepth 8, so no TRE0038 fires. Expansion materializes 20^7 (about 1.3e9) leaf references and about 6.7e7 AndNode arrays before Build counts the first node, so Compile runs for minutes or throws OutOfMemoryException instead of returning TRE0010. RuleDefinitions.ReadText on the same text does the same work and also allocates a path string for each node.
findings.expected_behavior: Expansion must count the nodes it produces against MaxNodeCount (or a dedicated budget) and stop with TRE0010 as soon as the budget is exceeded. RuleDefinitions.Reader needs the same bound.
findings.evidence:
I traced the path in DefinitionExpander.cs and RuleNodeCompiler.cs. I did not run the scenario or read RuleDefinitions.Reader. Neither file contains a size budget.

1. RuleNodeCompiler.Compile (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:88-95) calls DefinitionExpander.Expand(document, registry, options) first. Only after Expand returns does it call compiler.Build(root), which is where the report says MaxNodeCount is enforced. I did not open Build to check that. Expand itself has no counter and no early exit.

2. Expander.ExpandUse (DefinitionExpander.cs:213-300) is the only limit on a definition chain. It checks chain.Count >= options.MaxDefinitionDepth (line 277), which bounds how deep the chain goes. It does nothing about how many uses a body contains. A depth-7 chain of 20-way bodies passes that check, because the deepest use is made with chain.Count == 7 and 7 is below 8.

3. Line 299 calls this.ExpandNode(definition.Body, bound, nextChain, unused) for every use. Nothing caches or shares the result of an expansion. ExpandNode rebuilds each body node, for example AndNode via Carry(a, new AndNode(this.ExpandAll(...))) at line 134. ExpandAll (lines 197-211) allocates a new RuleNode[] for every operand list. Each use of d_k therefore re-expands and re-allocates d_k's whole body, so the work is fanout^depth. Only parameter substitution (line 124-127) and ConstantNode/TermNode/ErrorNode (line 132) are shared by reference, and that does not stop the repeated rebuilding.

4. For the scenario (`let d0 = p; let d1 = d0 AND x20; ... let d7 = d6 AND x20; d7`), each of the 20 uses of d_k expands a fresh d_k body. That gives about 20^6 (6.4e7) AndNode instances at the d1 level, each with its own 20-element array, and about 20^7 leaf references. That is many GB of allocation and minutes of CPU, or an OutOfMemoryException, before Build counts a single node. TRE0010 never gets a chance to fire.

I did not check the parser for a total-input size cap. The scenario text is only about 1.5 KB. The parser would have to cap the number of operands or definitions to stop it.

I did not read RuleDefinitions.Reader (RuleDefinitions.cs:263-332), so the ReadText half of the claim is unverified. The Compile half is traced.

findings.title: MaxNodeCount restarts at 0 inside every quantifier body, so the total node limit is not enforced
findings.summary: BuildQuantifier compiles the body through binding.CompileBody, which creates a new RuleNodeCompiler (CollectionBinding.cs:50-52) whose nodeCount starts at 0. Only depth, quantifier depth and the active variables are passed across the boundary. ADR-0010 (line 175) says 'a quantifier counts as one node plus its body, once', and CompilerOptions documents MaxNodeCount as the maximum total node count. In the code, each body gets its own full MaxNodeCount allowance, and the outer tree counts the whole quantifier as 1 node.
findings.failure_scenario: With the default MaxNodeCount 512: `FORALL(a IN items, <body of 500 nodes>) AND FORALL(b IN items, <500 nodes>) AND ...` with 20 such quantifiers compiles with no TRE0010, which gives a rule of about 10,000 nodes. A single quantifier with a 511-node body plus 511 outer nodes also passes, which is about 1,022 nodes.
findings.expected_behavior: Pass the running node count (or the remaining budget) into CompileBody the same way startDepth and startQuantifierDepth are passed, and add the body's count back to the outer total, so that TRE0010 fires when the combined tree exceeds MaxNodeCount.
findings.evidence: I traced the path. RuleNodeCompiler.cs:425-432 (BuildQuantifier) calls binding.CompileBody and passes only this.options, depth + 1, this.quantifierDepth and this.activeVariables. It does not pass the running nodeCount or the remaining budget. CollectionBinding.cs:50-52 builds a fresh RuleNodeCompiler through the static RuleNodeCompiler<Element<...>>.Compile(body, elementRegistry, bodyOptions, depth, quantifierDepth, enclosingVariables). The nodeCount field (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:27) therefore starts at 0 in that new compiler. Build (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:205-206) increments the count and compares it to options.MaxNodeCount, and the body compiler's options still carry the full 512. After CompileBody returns, only bodyDiagnostics are merged (line 436) and the body's count is never added back to the outer total. The outer compiler counts the quantifier as one node. TRE0010 is raised only in Build, so no later check can catch the combined tree. ADR-0010 line 175 says a quantifier counts as one node plus its body, once, and CompilerOptions documents MaxNodeCount as the maximum total node count. The code gives each body its own full allowance, so the scenario works as described. For example, 20 quantifiers with 500-node bodies each never hit the limit, and a 511-node body plus 511 outer nodes passes. I did not run a test. The behavior is a bypass of a compile-time structural limit. It is not a correctness bug in evaluation. The limit is also not the only protection, because MaxDepth and MaxQuantifierDepth are propagated. Nested quantifiers still give each level a fresh 512, so growth is bounded only by depth. Severity is medium: a resource-limit bypass that matters mainly for untrusted rule authors.

findings.title: Lenient literal guessing silently changes or drops argument values (data loss on tool conversion)
findings.summary: Guess, which builds the TermIdentity of an unregistered predicate in Lenient mode, ignores the TryParse results. A number without '.' that does not fit in a long (exponent form or too large) becomes Int64 0. A decimal that fails to parse becomes 0. A mixed-kind array is coerced: a later element of a different kind is turned into a string, and when OfArray then rejects the mixed array, the catch at 164-171 returns an EMPTY string array. docs/tool-core.md:105-107 says the Lenient tool compiler 'accepts every argument as written' and that conversion keeps the tree. Printers only see the compiled TermIdentity, so the original value is lost. Different terms can also collapse to the same identity, which misleads the analyzer.
findings.failure_scenario: The tool converts JSON `{"predicate":"limit","args":{"max":1e5}}` to rule text as `limit(max: 0)`. `{"args":{"id":99999999999999999999}}` becomes `id: 0`. `levels: [1, 2.5]` becomes `levels: []`. `tags: ["a", 1]` becomes `["a", "1"]`. `foo(n: 1e5) AND NOT foo(n: 0)` is analyzed as `t AND NOT t`, which gives a spurious contradiction warning.
findings.expected_behavior: In Lenient mode, keep the literal exactly as written: keep the text of a number that has no exact numeric kind, keep each element's kind, or report a diagnostic. Never fall back silently to 0 or to an empty array.
findings.evidence: I traced the code and did not run it. LiteralConversion.Guess (src/TruthWeaver/Compilation/LiteralConversion.cs:80-89) discards the results of decimal.TryParse and long.TryParse, so a failed parse leaves the default 0. A number text with no '.' that is not a valid long (JSON raw text "1e5" or "99999999999999999999") becomes OfInt64(0). Raw number text really does reach Guess: JsonNodeCursor.cs:125 uses element.GetRawText(), YamlNodeCursor.cs:145 and DslParser.cs:907 pass the text through, and RuleNodeCompiler.cs:169 calls Guess for every argument of an unregistered predicate in Lenient mode to build the TermIdentity. GuessArray (lines 149-172) coerces any element whose kind differs from the first element to OfString(elements[i].Text ?? ""). For [1, 2.5], the first element is Int64 and the second becomes the string "2.5". LiteralValue.OfArray (src/TruthWeaver.Abstractions/LiteralValue.cs:126-139) throws ArgumentException on the kind mismatch. The catch at lines 168-171 then returns an empty StringArray. For ["a", 1], the 1 becomes the string "1" and the kind changes silently. Nested arrays have no Text, so they become "". docs/tool-core.md:105 says the lenient compiler "accepts every argument as written", which these paths contradict. The collapse of different terms into one identity follows directly. Both foo(n: 1e5) and foo(n: 0) get Int64 0, so the identities are equal and the analyzer sees the same term. I did not trace the exact printer output of the converter or the analyzer's contradiction warning. Impact is limited to unregistered predicates in Lenient mode, which is the tool path. Registered predicates use TryConvert, which reports a diagnostic. Real silent data loss and false analyzer results happen only for unusual literals: exponent form, a number beyond long range, or mixed-kind arrays.

findings.title: Definitions not reachable from the rule body are never validated: cycles, unknown uses and operator errors inside them compile silently
findings.summary: Expand only walks document.Body. A definition body is checked only when a reachable use expands it. docs/rule-text.md:102-103 states unconditionally that 'A definition cannot reference itself, directly or through a chain of other definitions', and ADR-0008 decision 6 lists cycles and unknown definitions as compile errors. A document whose unused definitions are cyclic or broken still compiles, and the problem appears only when a later edit first uses the definition. With the default Lints = None, the author gets no message at all.
findings.failure_scenario: `let a = b; let b = a; let c = AND(x); isAdmin` compiles successfully with no TRE0036, TRE0006 or other diagnostic. Changing the body to `isAdmin AND a` then fails with a cycle that existed all along.
findings.expected_behavior: Report the cycle and unknown-definition guardrails for every declared definition, whether or not it is used, or document that only definitions reachable from the rule are checked.

findings.title: Repeated parameter names in a let definition are accepted and the last argument silently wins
findings.summary: Neither DslParser.ParseDefinition (DslParser.cs:767-779) nor the expander rejects a definition whose parameter list repeats a name (compared case-insensitively). When the expander binds the arguments, the later entry overwrites the earlier one in a case-insensitive dictionary, so one argument is discarded with no diagnostic. This contradicts the compiler's own rule for repeated predicate arguments (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:750, 'A repeated name never wins silently', TRE duplicate-argument error).
findings.failure_scenario: `let pick(x, X) = x; pick(isAdmin, isGuest)` compiles to `isGuest` with no diagnostic, so the author's first argument is dropped.
findings.expected_behavior: A definition that declares the same parameter name twice is a compile error, in the same family as DuplicateArgument or DefinitionNameCollision.

findings.title: RuleDefinitions.SourcesOf hard-codes the default MaxDefinitionDepth and disagrees with compiles that use another limit
findings.summary: Reader.ExpandUse mirrors the expander's refusals but uses CompilerOptions.Default.MaxDefinitionDepth (8), and RuleDefinitions takes no options. A host that compiles with a different MaxDefinitionDepth gets a source map that does not match the tree it compiled.
findings.failure_scenario: The host compiles with `new CompilerOptions(MaxDefinitionDepth: 12)` a document whose chain is 10 definitions deep. The compiled rule contains the expanded nodes, but `RuleDefinitions.ReadText(text).SourcesOf("$.operands[0]...")` stops at depth 8. It returns empty or truncated source lists for the deeper nodes, so an editor that maps compiled nodes back to their let definitions points at the wrong place or at nothing.
findings.expected_behavior: Read*/SourcesOf accept the CompilerOptions that were used to compile, or use the same limit as the expander.

findings.title: BETWEEN bound errors point at the whole node instead of its min/max member
findings.summary: An InvalidThresholdValue for BETWEEN uses `path: node.Path`, but the threshold family points at its 'k' member (line 631, PathOf(node, "k")). For JSON and YAML, LocateInJson therefore gives the span of the whole between object, not the offending bound.
findings.failure_scenario: `{"op":"between","min":3,"max":1,"operands":[...]}` reports TRE0008 with the span of the whole object, while `{"op":"atLeast","k":9,...}` reports the span of the `k` value.
findings.expected_behavior: Point at `min` or `max`, whichever violates the rule (for example `max` when max > n or min > max), the same way threshold errors point at `k`.

reviewers.label: F4 Evaluation
reviewers.coverage:
I read all of Evaluator.cs, EvaluationState.cs, CompiledRule.Evaluation.cs, CompiledRule.cs, EvaluationOptions.cs, BatchEvaluator.cs, DecisionExplainer.cs and TraceText.cs. For context I also read CollectionBinding.EvaluateQuantifierAsync, K3Logic, ExpressionShape, PredicateRegistry, OperatorDefinitions, PolicySet.EvaluateAsync/RunAsync, ADR-0002 in full, docs/strong-k3/specification/evaluation.md, docs/diagnostics.md (limits table) and the ADR-0010 fault-budget lines. I did not read ADR-0001, ADR-0005 or ADR-0006 in full; I relied on ADR-0002 and the evaluation spec for fault and cancellation rules. I did not fully read, in src/TruthWeaver/Evaluation: CompiledRule.Printing.cs, CompiledRule.Rewrites.cs, CompiledRule.RuleText.cs, RuleCoverage*.cs, ShadowReplay*.cs, DecisionRecord.cs, VariableConversion.cs, or the small option/record files (ExplainOptions, NormalFormOptions, OutlineNode, RewriteLaw, RewriteStep, SimplifyResult, SourceAnswer, TermCoverage, NodeCoverage, RuleIdentity, RuleMetrics, ElementEvaluationLimitExceededException, TestDoubleMisuseException, NoServiceProvider, DecisionJsonOptions). Those are printing, rewrites and coverage, not evaluation semantics.

Checked and found no problem: the K3 truth tables in K3Logic; AND/OR/COALESCE/If short-circuit and Exhaustive branches; cardinality and Between folds; inspection; memo scoping; Lenient unknown-predicate faults; class-based predicate resolution faults; the OCE catch filter for predicates, data sources and selectors (it uses the linked timeout token, as ADR-0002 requires); TestDoubleMisuseException escaping. Concurrency: CompiledRule holds only readonly fields plus Lazy<T> (thread-safe by default) over an immutable registry and tree. Each EvaluateAsync builds a fresh Evaluator and EvaluationState, so FaultBudget is per evaluation even in parallel EvaluateManyAsync. BatchEvaluator cancels and drains the evaluations in flight. The shared-state internal overload is only used one rule after another by PolicySet, so its non-thread-safe dictionaries are not raced.

findings.title: Fault-budget abort drops skipped AND/OR/COALESCE and quantifier operands from the fold, so an aborted evaluation can return a definite (even True) result
findings.summary: Once state.Aborted is set, EvalChainAsync marks the remaining operands NotEvaluated and continues without combining Unknown into the accumulator. CollectionBinding.EvaluateQuantifierAsync (src/TruthWeaver/Registry/CollectionBinding.cs:162) does the same for the remaining elements. Whatever the fold reached before the abort is returned as if the skipped operands could not change it. docs/diagnostics.md:170 says the terms not yet run count as Unknown. The non-chain operators get this right: they go through EvalAsync, which returns Unknown at Evaluator.cs:140.
findings.failure_scenario: FaultBudget = 1, rule `IsUnknown(boom) AND isOff` (boom throws). IsUnknown(boom) is True and the abort fires. isOff is skipped and never folded, so Result = True and IsSatisfied = true: the check fails open. Without a budget the result is False, and per the docs it should be AND(True, Unknown) = Unknown. Same with `AtMost(5, boom) AND isOff`, and with `EXISTS(x IN items: boomOrTrue)` where element 0 faults: the result is False although element 1 was never run.
findings.evidence:
Traced. Evaluator.cs:657-659 sets state.Aborted = true when Faults.Count >= FaultBudget. EvalChainAsync (Evaluator.cs:486-494) then takes the `stop || this.state.Aborted` branch for each remaining operand. It only adds a NotEvaluated trace node and `continue`s, so it never runs `accumulator = combine(accumulator, Unknown)` (line 498). The accumulator therefore stays at whatever the fold reached.

Scenario `IsUnknown(boom) AND isOff` with FaultBudget=1: boom throws, so a fault is recorded and the budget aborts. IsUnknown(Unknown) returns True (a normal evaluation, since EvalAsync checked Aborted before the term ran), and the AND accumulator becomes True. isOff is skipped without being combined. The chain returns True. Decision.IsSatisfied (Decision.cs:33) is just `Result == True`, so it returns true. It does not check Faults or an aborted flag. By the docs, the skipped operand is Unknown, so AND(True, Unknown) = Unknown.

CollectionBinding.cs:162-167 does the same for quantifier elements on abort. Its comment at lines 145-148 shows the behavior is deliberate: the fold keeps what it reached ("exactly as today"). This contradicts docs/diagnostics.md:170 and CompilerOptions.cs:16 (unrun terms are Unknown). The MaxElementEvaluations path forces Unknown at lines 215-218, but the fault-budget path has no such fix. Non-chain operators go through EvalAsync, which returns Unknown at lines 140-148, so they are correct. A skipped AND/OR/COALESCE operand and a skipped element are the inconsistent cases. For OR, `IsUnknown(boom) OR x` aborting early gives False where Unknown is correct. For AND, a True partial fold gives a fail-open True.

Severity: the defect is real and fail-open, but it only triggers when the caller opts into FaultBudget and the rule has an external operator (IsUnknown, IsFalse and so on) over a faulting term. The result carries Faults, and the false-negative direction (False instead of Unknown) is fail-closed. I rate it high, not critical.

findings.title: With FaultBudget set, Exhaustive mode changes Decision.Result, against the ADR-0002 invariant
findings.summary: ADR-0002 and docs/strong-k3/specification/evaluation.md say Exhaustive mode never changes Result. Exhaustive runs terms that ShortCircuit skips, so it records more faults and reaches the budget sooner. The abort then skips operands that would have settled the result. No doc states which rule wins when the two options are combined.
findings.failure_scenario: FaultBudget = 1, rule `(isOn OR boom) AND isOff`. ShortCircuit: the OR stops at isOn, boom never runs, isOff gives False. Exhaustive: boom runs and faults, the abort skips isOff, and Result is True with the current drop bug (Unknown even after that bug is fixed). The two modes give different results for the same input.
findings.evidence:
I traced the scenario `(isOn OR boom) AND isOff` with FaultBudget=1. It does give different Results in the two modes.

- RecordFault (Evaluator.cs:650-661) sets state.Aborted = true once Faults.Count >= budget.
- ShortCircuit: the inner OR stops at isOn (Evaluator.cs:499-502), so boom never runs and no fault is recorded. The outer AND then runs isOff and returns False.
- Exhaustive: the OR does not stop (`!exhaustive && stops(...)` is false), so boom runs and faults. The budget is reached and Aborted becomes true.
- The outer AND loop (Evaluator.cs:488-494) then marks isOff as NotEvaluated and continues. It does not feed that operand into the accumulator, so AND(True, skipped) stays True. Result is True in Exhaustive and False in ShortCircuit.
- This contradicts docs/adr/0002-evaluation-semantics.md:141-145 and docs/strong-k3/specification/evaluation.md:29. Both say Exhaustive never changes Result, and ADR-0002 says the invariant must hold for any future change.
- Neither document says how FaultBudget interacts with Exhaustive. evaluation.md:23 only says the budget stops evaluation at the Nth fault.
- Two aspects are separate from this finding. Dropping aborted operands lets an abort produce a definite, even fail-open True, and that is a distinct defect. Also, the budget abort makes Result order- and mode-dependent whenever it fires.
- Even with the drop bug fixed (aborted operands counted as Unknown), Exhaustive would give Unknown and ShortCircuit would give False. So the mode-dependence stays.

I rate it medium rather than high. It needs the opt-in FaultBudget together with Exhaustive, which is documented as diagnostic/support use. The fail-open True comes from the separate drop bug.

findings.title: TermIdentities omits collection identities, so PolicySet silently drops selector, element-limit and missing-collection faults
findings.summary: CollectTermIdentities only collects TermExpression identities (it does walk into quantifier bodies). A collection-level fault is recorded under TermIdentity(collectionName, []): a throwing selector (CollectionBinding.cs:111), MaxElementEvaluations (CollectionBinding.cs:173) and an unregistered collection (Evaluator.cs:437). PolicySet.RunAsync keeps only the faults whose Term is in rule.TermIdentities (PolicySet{TContext}.cs:174), so these faults never reach the PolicyDecision.
findings.failure_scenario: A policy condition `FORALL(x IN lines: ok)` whose `lines` selector throws evaluates to Unknown. The policy set returns Indeterminate with an empty Faults list, so the caller cannot see why. The same happens when MaxElementEvaluations is exceeded.

findings.title: The flat trace logs no operator nodes, but CONTEXT.md and EvaluationOptions.IncludeTrace say it does
findings.summary: AddTraceEntry is called only for constants, terms, quantifiers and skipped nodes. A visited NOT/AND/OR/XOR/threshold/If node only adds a TraceNode. CONTEXT.md:37 says the flat log has 'one entry per node visited or skipped', and the IncludeTrace doc (EvaluationOptions.cs:34) says 'every term and operator'. A test pins the leaves-only shape (EvaluationOptionsTests.cs:48 expects ["a", "b"]), so the docs look wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller evaluates `a AND b` with IncludeTrace and expects an `AND` entry in Decision.Trace, as the docs promise. Only `a` and `b` appear, so a tool that rebuilds operator results from the flat log finds none.

findings.title: Collection-level faults skip RecordFault: no log, no fault metric
findings.summary: A throwing selector and the MaxElementEvaluations fault add directly to state.Faults. Evaluator.RecordFault (Evaluator.cs:650) is the path that also writes EvaluationLog.PredicateFaulted and calls TruthWeaverMetrics.FaultRecorded. Its budget check is copied inline instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A collection selector throws in production. The Decision carries the fault, but no log line is written and the truthweaver fault counter does not increase, so dashboards under-report faults.

findings.title: Timeout and MaxElementEvaluations are not validated; Timeout is cooperative only
findings.summary: FaultBudget below 1 is rejected up front. A negative Timeout (other than -1 ms) or one above int.MaxValue ms only fails inside CancelAfter, with an undocumented ArgumentOutOfRangeException. In EvaluateManyAsync that happens during enumeration, not at the call as the docs promise for bad options. MaxElementEvaluations <= 0 is accepted, and every quantifier then faults. The timeout is only noticed at the next token check, so a predicate that blocks synchronously and ignores the token runs past the 'overall wall-clock bound'.
findings.failure_scenario: EvaluationOptions(Timeout: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(-5)) passed to EvaluateManyAsync throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException from CancelAfter on the first MoveNextAsync. Separately, a Timeout of 1 s with a predicate doing a 30 s blocking call returns only after 30 s.

findings.title: Evaluator hard-codes operator trace labels instead of reading OperatorDefinitions
findings.summary: Evaluated nodes get literal labels ("AND", "OR", "COALESCE", "XOR", "PARITY", "ExactlyOne", and $"{OpName}({K})" for thresholds). Skipped nodes go through TraceText.Of, which reads OperatorDefinitions.Label. CLAUDE.md says the Evaluator trace labels come from that table, and RuleCoverageAccumulator compares trace text against TraceText output.
findings.failure_scenario: A change to the PARITY label in OperatorDefinitions (for example "Parity") changes skipped nodes and coverage text, but evaluated nodes still say "PARITY". Trace tree labels then disagree, and coverage matching against the trace breaks.

reviewers.label: F5 Analysis+Rewriting
reviewers.coverage: Fully read: Analysis/Analyzer.cs, BddManager.cs, Linter.cs, RuleEquivalence.cs, RuleImplication.cs, RuleCounterfactual.cs, ChangeSetSearch.cs, RuleSetAnalysis.cs (lines 110-260); Rewriting/Simplifier.cs, Canonicalizer.cs, Compressor.cs, NormalForms.cs, NandNorExpander.cs, ThresholdExpansion.cs, PrimitiveExpander.cs, OrderOptimizer.cs, ExpressionTools.cs, XorForm.cs, EquivalentForm.cs, IfForm.cs, ParityForm.cs, InspectionForm.cs, Forms.cs; Ast/ThresholdSemantics.cs, NodeShape.cs, QuantifierAtom.cs; Evaluation/CompiledRule.Rewrites.cs; ADR-0010 decisions 8-9; ADR-0009 decision 5; the monotonicity statements in docs/strong-k3. Not read or only skimmed: RuleOverlap.cs, TermValuation.cs, RuleSet.cs, RuleSetAnalysis.cs lines 1-109, the small result/outcome records (ChangeSet, TermChange, *Outcome, *Result, ValueProfile, JointOutcome, CounterfactualOptions, BddNodeBudgetExceededException), and Rewriting/RewriteTrace.cs, RewriteOutcome.cs, ThresholdConnectives.cs. Checked and found correct under K3: dual-rail encoding (d, d OR q); NOT/AND/OR/XOR/EQUIVALENT/IMPLIES/NAND/NOR/PARITY/If/COALESCE/inspection rails; AtLeast/AtMost/Exactly/Between interval semantics; ValueNode; Witness readback; Cofactor/Restrict precondition; all Simplifier laws (identity, annihilator, absorption, negated pairs, threshold shift and fold, COALESCE truncation, IsDefinite with quantifiers); Canonicalizer aliases; every Compressor pattern; NNF De Morgan for thresholds and quantifiers; CNF/DNF distribution and caps; NAND/NOR identities; the lint replacements; redundancy and shadowing against docs/rewriting-rules.md. Termination: the rewrite loops are bounded by MaxPasses (8 or 16, with an 8-round inner loop in the Simplifier) and report RewriteNotConverged. I found no rewrite cycle. I did not run any build or test; the AtLeastBdd call counts were computed with a standalone recurrence.

findings.title: AtLeastBdd recursion is exponential in operand count, so Compile can hang
findings.summary: AtLeastBdd recurses twice per operand without memoizing on (k, fromIndex). The BDD ite cache absorbs the node work, but the number of calls is about C(n, k). The only cap is on distinct terms (MaxAnalysisTerms). Operand count is not capped, and the compiler does not reject repeated threshold operands. This path runs on every Compile (Analyze, the Analyze step of ADR-0003). It also runs in Linter.Profile, RuleMetrics.BddNodeCount, RuleEquivalence, RuleOverlap and RuleSetAnalysis. The 100,000 node budget does not trip, because the node count stays small; only the call count grows.
findings.failure_scenario: Compile `AtLeast(20, a1..a20, a1..a20)`: 41 nodes, under MaxNodeCount 512, and 20 distinct terms, so within the default cap. AtLeastBdd makes about 5.4e11 calls per rail (computed from T(m,k)=1+T(m-1,k-1)+T(m-1,k)), so Compile does not return. Even 30 operands with k=15 costs about 6e8 calls per rail, which is minutes. A service that compiles user-written rule text can be stalled this way.
findings.expected_behavior: Memoize AtLeastBdd on (k, fromIndex), or build the threshold as the standard O(n*k) dynamic-programming BDD, so the cost is polynomial in the operand count.
findings.evidence:
Traced in src/TruthWeaver/Analysis/Analyzer.cs. AtLeastBdd (lines 710-726) has no memo on (k, fromIndex). Every call that is not a base case (k<=0 or k>remaining) makes two recursive calls, at lines 723 and 724: one with (k-1, i+1) and one with (k, i+1). So the call count follows T(m,k)=1+T(m-1,k-1)+T(m-1,k), which grows roughly like C(n,k). The BDD operations are cached, but the calls themselves are not. AtLeast (702-708) runs this on both rails. Threshold (738-749) calls AtLeast once or twice.

Analyze (33-52) only checks distinct terms against MaxAnalysisTerms (default 20). It then calls Build unconditionally. Operand count is not limited: OperatorDefinitions.cs lines 126-130 give AtLeast, AtMost, GreaterThan, LessThan and Exactly a MaxOperands of null. The only other bound is MaxNodeCount, 512 by default. That allows about 40 repeated operands, so the 20-distinct-term cap does not stop it. I did not confirm that the Build threshold case or Compile calls Analyze on every compile. The Analyze entry point and the unbounded operands are confirmed.

A rule such as AtLeast(20, a1..a20, a1..a20) therefore reaches about 1e11 calls per rail and Compile does not return in practice. The ALL case is not affected: k=n prunes immediately, so it stays linear. Duplicated operands are needed to reach the extreme cases, but 30 operands with k=15 already costs about 1e8 calls.

Severity: this is a real denial of service when untrusted rule text is compiled. It needs a deliberately crafted rule, and it is fixed with a small change (memoize on (k, fromIndex)). I would rate it medium to high and keep it at high only if the engine takes untrusted authoring input.

findings.title: ExpandToNand / ExpandToNor throw on any rule that contains FORALL or EXISTS
findings.summary: PrimitiveExpander.ExpandTop returns a QuantifierExpression unchanged, as ADR-0010 decision 9 specifies. NandNorExpander.Convert has no QuantifierExpression case, so it reaches the default arm and throws InvalidOperationException. ADR-0010 decision 9 and docs/rewriting-rules.md:11 say the quantifier stays an atom and its body is rewritten in place. The public ExpandToNand contract also says the method never throws for a normal rule. No test covers ExpandToNand or ExpandToNor with a quantifier.
findings.failure_scenario: `compiled("a AND FORALL(x IN items, elementTrue)").ExpandToNand()` passes the size and SubsetCost checks. Convert then hits the FORALL node and throws `InvalidOperationException: Unhandled expression type 'QuantifierExpression'`. The caller should get a NAND rule with `FORALL(x IN items, <NAND form of the body>)` kept as an atom.
findings.expected_behavior: Add a QuantifierExpression case that keeps the quantifier and converts its body: new QuantifierExpression(q.Kind, q.Variable, q.CollectionName, Convert(q.Body, conversion)).
findings.evidence: I traced the path and found no guard on it. CompiledRule.Rewrites.cs:68-71 sends ExpandToNand straight to NandNorExpander.ToNand(this.Root, cap), which calls Rewrite (NandNorExpander.cs:60). Rewrite calls PrimitiveExpander.Expand(node) at line 62. Expand maps the children first and then calls ExpandTop (PrimitiveExpander.cs:25). ExpandTop returns a QuantifierExpression unchanged (PrimitiveExpander.cs:69), and its body is already expanded because ExpressionTools.MapChildren handles quantifiers (ExpressionTools.cs:171). The size check and SubsetCost then run. Neither special-cases quantifiers, and SubsetCost goes through ExpressionTools.Children. Convert (NandNorExpander.cs:121-138) has cases only for Constant/Term, Not, And, Or, Coalesce and Threshold. A QuantifierExpression reaches the default arm at line 136 and throws InvalidOperationException("Unhandled expression type 'QuantifierExpression'"). The comment there, "PrimitiveExpander has already removed every other node type", is wrong for quantifiers. The same Convert serves ExpandToNor. I did not run the code, but the trace is complete. The impact is an unhandled exception from a public API, which the docs say never throws for a normal rule. The fix is the one proposed: add a QuantifierExpression case that rebuilds the node with a converted body. Severity is high rather than critical because it only affects rules that contain FORALL or EXISTS, and it fails loudly instead of returning a wrong result.

findings.title: Quantifier atoms keyed by text make RuleEquivalence call valid ToNnf rewrites NotEquivalent
findings.summary: The analyzer gives each quantifier an independent, fully free pair of BDD variables, keyed by its canonical text. ToNnf rewrites `NOT FORALL(x IN c, b)` to `EXISTS(x IN c, NOT b)`, which ADR-0010 decision 9 states is an identity, but the two texts become two unrelated atoms. RuleEquivalence.Compare (RuleEquivalence.cs:65-72) then returns a definite NotEquivalent with a counterexample that no collection can produce. It should return Equivalent, or Undecided at least. The comment at Analyzer.cs:805-806 says "every K3 value of the atom is reachable". That is also false: `FORALL(x IN c, True)` is never False and `EXISTS(x IN c, False)` is never True. docs/rewriting-rules.md:402 calls the check "sound", but a NotEquivalent or DoesNotHold verdict across quantifiers is only a candidate.
findings.failure_scenario: Compile `r = NOT FORALL(x IN items, elementTrue)` and compare it with `r.ToNnf()`, which gives `EXISTS(x IN items, NOT elementTrue)`. RuleEquivalence.Compare returns NotEquivalent with a counterexample that makes one atom True and the other False. So one engine layer (ToNnf) and another (RuleEquivalence) disagree on the same rule. A Testing-package rewrite assertion built on RuleEquivalence would also fail for this valid rewrite.
findings.expected_behavior: When a difference depends only on quantifier atoms, report Undecided (or flag the counterexample as unverified) instead of NotEquivalent. Otherwise, normalize quantifier atoms (for example push negations to the NNF form) before keying them. Correct the soundness claim in the comment and in the docs.
findings.evidence:
I traced the path in the code and the claim holds.

1. `NormalForms.cs:276-286` (NnfBuilder.VisitCore) rewrites `NOT FORALL(x IN c, b)` to `EXISTS(x IN c, NOT b)`. It flips the kind and negates the body. This matches ADR-0010 decision 9 and docs/rewriting-rules.md:390.

2. `Analyzer.cs:803-817` builds each QuantifierExpression as an atom with two free BDD variables. They are keyed by `QuantifierAtom.IdentityOf(q)` (`Ast/QuantifierAtom.cs:18-21`), which is `CanonicalPrinter.Print(node)`. That text includes the kind and the body. `FORALL(x IN c, b)` and `EXISTS(x IN c, NOT b)` therefore get different text and different, unrelated variable pairs.

3. `RuleEquivalence.Compare` (`RuleEquivalence.cs:55-72`) has no quantifier handling. It calls `Analyzer.FindDifference`. It then returns `NotEquivalent` with a counterexample keyed by the printed atom text. The atoms are independent, so setting A1=True and A2=True separates `NOT A1` from `A2`. The two rules are semantically identical.

4. The comment at `Analyzer.cs:805-806` ("every K3 value of the atom is reachable ... so this is sound") is false. `FORALL(x IN c, True)` is never False, and `EXISTS(x IN c, False)` is never True. The BDD still treats every value of each atom as reachable, and ignores the relation between atoms.

5. docs/rewriting-rules.md:402 and ADR-0010 line 219 say the check is "sound, incomplete". That is correct only for `Equivalent`. `NotEquivalent` or `DoesNotHold` across quantifier atoms is a false negative. The ADR admits incompleteness across differently written bodies. It does not admit that the verdict can be a definite wrong "NotEquivalent".

Impact: no crash, no wrong rule evaluation, and no security effect. The effect is a misleading analysis verdict. A Testing-package rewrite assertion built on RuleEquivalence would fail for a valid ToNnf rewrite. I did not run it. I only traced the code. The documented incompleteness lowers the severity.

findings.title: NormalForms keeps If as an atom as if it were not monotone, but the K3 reference says it is a monotone connective
findings.summary: NormalForms groups IfExpression with COALESCE and the inspections as "not information-monotone". So it pushes no NOT into an If and never distributes an If in CNF or DNF. docs/strong-k3/functions/if.md:16, the glossary and CLAUDE.md say If is a Strong Kleene connective (monotone), and IfForm.Build gives an exact AND/OR/NOT definition. NandNorExpander already uses that definition. docs/rewriting-rules.md:320 repeats the wrong classification, so the code and that page disagree with the K3 reference.
findings.failure_scenario: `ToNnf("NOT If(c, a, b)")` returns `NOT If(c, a, b)` unchanged. Under the K3 reference this is not negation normal form, because NOT sits above a connective. The NNF is `(NOT c OR NOT a) AND (c OR NOT b) AND (NOT a OR NOT b)`. ToCnf and ToDnf likewise return a tree with an If inside a clause, so the result is not CNF or DNF.
findings.expected_behavior: Expand If through IfForm (via the default PrimitiveExpander.ExpandTop arm) like the other derived connectives. Keep only COALESCE, the inspections and quantifiers as atoms, and correct docs/rewriting-rules.md:320.

findings.title: Compile-time analysis and the other BDD readers run with no node budget
findings.summary: Analyze (line 50), TargetFunction (140, used by counterfactual search), Profile (185, used by the lints), BddNodeCount (208, used by RuleMetrics) and CreateValuation (415) all build `new BddManager()` with no budget. Their only bound is the distinct-term cap. Variables are ordered by first occurrence and are never reordered. When a host raises MaxAnalysisTerms, a rule whose first-occurrence order is bad can make Compile build an exponential BDD. There is no diagnostic when this happens: TRE0011 covers only the term count. The BddManager comment (lines 24-29) says the node budget is "the only guard that bounds time", but the pipeline step that runs on every compile has no such guard.
findings.failure_scenario: Set CompilerOptions.MaxAnalysisTerms = 48 and compile `(x1 AND ... AND x24 AND False) OR (x1 AND y1) OR ... OR (x24 AND y24)`. The constant-False conjunct puts x1..x24 ahead of every y in the order, and `OR(xi AND yi)` under that order needs about 2^24 nodes per rail. Compile then allocates gigabytes instead of returning an info diagnostic.
findings.expected_behavior: Give the compile-time and metric builds a node budget too. When the budget trips, catch BddNodeBudgetExceededException and return the TRE0011-style "analysis skipped" info diagnostic, or null for Profile and BddNodeCount.

reviewers.label: F6 Predicates A
reviewers.coverage:
I read all of NumericPredicates.cs (1279 lines), StringPredicates.cs and CollectionPredicates.cs. I also fully read the shared helpers they depend on: ScalarPredicateCore.cs, PredicateResult.cs, NullBehaviorScope.cs, NullBehavior.cs and ScalarKinds.cs. Docs read: docs/strong-k3/predicates/README.md (shared null, twin, kind and family rules), collection-setequals.md, collection-notsetequals.md, collection-containsall.md, string-isequalto.md and numeric-isbetween.md, ADR-0006 decisions 1-13, and the label, argument-name, null-element and empty-argument lines of every numeric, string and collection page (checked with Grep, not read end to end).

K3 contract checks with no defect found:
- Null selection answers Unknown by default and False only under NullBehavior.False.
- Every NotX twin is the exact Strong Kleene complement, null included (ForNullAsync negates).
- The null tests are definite.
- SetEquals/NotSetEquals read a null collection as the empty set under NullBehavior.False, as their pages and NullBehavior.False's XML doc document.
- Reversed bounds are checked before the selector and throw ArgumentException, which becomes a fault.
- Selector and argument exceptions propagate to the evaluator as faults.
- All string and collection comparisons are Ordinal or OrdinalIgnoreCase, with no culture dependence. Trim is culture-independent.
- Empty-argument semantics match the docs.
- Duplicate argument names (for example argumentName "trim" on string IsEqualTo) are rejected by PredicateRegistryBuilder, per the PredicateSchemaFile comment.

Not applicable in this slice: regex cost limits (no regex in these files; RegexPredicates is another slice) and predicate-owned timeouts or cancellation (every delegate is synchronous and ignores the CancellationToken, which is acceptable for O(n+m) work).

Not fully read: ADR-0001, ADR-0002 and ADR-0005 (I relied on the CLAUDE.md summary and the predicates README fault table), the specification/*.md pages, and the individual numeric, string and collection pages beyond the Grep-checked lines.

findings.title: Numeric IsBetween/IsNotBetween default labels do not match the reference pages
findings.summary: Both IsBetween overloads default `label` to "IsBetween" (lines 806, 844), and both IsNotBetween overloads default it to "Not IsBetween" (lines 884, 924). numeric-isbetween.md:8 and numeric-isnotbetween.md:8 give the labels as `Is Between` and `Is Not Between`. Every other numeric factory follows the spaced "Is X" pattern that its page shows. The code side is wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: A host registers `NumericPredicates.IsBetween("quantityBetween", c => c.Qty)` without a label. The registry schema, and every UI, trace or explain output that reads `PredicateSchema.Label`, shows "IsBetween" where the reference page promises "Is Between". IsNotBetween shows "Not IsBetween" where the page promises "Is Not Between".
findings.expected_behavior: Default labels "Is Between" and "Is Not Between", as in the docs and the other numeric factories.

findings.title: Predicates index says a null element has no effect outside HasCount, but IsSubsetOf and SetEquals answer False because of one
findings.summary: The index says a repeated element and a `null` element 'have no effect on the other predicates'. For IsSubsetOf, IsNotSubsetOf, SetEquals and NotSetEquals, a null element changes the answer. The code (CollectionPredicates.cs:473 `selected.All(set.Contains)` and :983-987 `HashSet.SetEquals`) and those predicates' own pages (collection-issubsetof.md:61/69, collection-setequals.md:62/73) agree on this. The index sentence is the wrong side.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader trusts the index and expects `tagsIsSubsetOf(values: ["admin"])` with `tags = ["admin", null]` to be True, because the null element supposedly has no effect. The engine answers False, as does `tagsSetEquals(values: ["admin"])` for the same input.
findings.expected_behavior: The index sentence limits 'no effect' to Contains/ContainsAny/ContainsAll and their twins. It states that a null element is an extra member for IsSubsetOf and SetEquals and their twins.

findings.title: Collection HasCount predicates accept a negative count with no diagnostic
findings.summary: The ten HasCount* factories (lines 534-862) build the schema through `Build`, which sets no `ArgumentValidator`. A negative `count` literal compiles cleanly. Because `Count` is never negative, the term is then a constant for every non-null collection. Range predicates catch a comparable authoring error (reversed bounds) with TRE0026, but this one passes silently. The docs do not say what a negative count means.
findings.failure_scenario: `tagsHasCountLessThan(count: -1)` compiles with no diagnostic and answers False for every non-null collection. `tagsHasCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(count: -1)` answers True for every non-null collection, so a typo turns a gate into an always-pass rule, with no error at compile or evaluation time.
findings.expected_behavior: A negative literal count is reported at compile time through an ArgumentValidator (for example TRE0026, as for reversed bounds). A negative count from a data source is an argument fault. Otherwise the docs state the constant-answer behavior.

findings.title: Factories do not reject a null selector at registration; every evaluation faults instead
findings.summary: None of the Numeric, String or Collection factories calls `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(selector)`. The only null check in the package is the one on `timeProvider` (DateTimePredicates.cs:452). A null selector is captured in the delegate and throws NullReferenceException on each evaluation. The evaluator turns that into Unknown plus a Fault per ADR-0001, so a host wiring bug looks like a runtime data fault and is never a registration error.
findings.failure_scenario: A host builds its selector from configuration or reflection and passes `null!` to `StringPredicates.StartsWith("codeStartsWith", selector)`. Registration and compile succeed. Every `codeStartsWith(value: "A")` evaluation is Unknown with a NullReferenceException fault, and IsSatisfied fails closed for all requests. Nothing points to the registration as the cause.
findings.expected_behavior: Each factory throws ArgumentNullException for a null `selector` (and `name`) when it is called, as DateTimePredicates does for `timeProvider`.

reviewers.label: F7 Predicates B
reviewers.coverage:
I read every file in the slice in full: TypePredicates.cs, ScalarPredicates.cs, ScalarPredicateCore.cs, ScalarKind.cs, ScalarKinds.cs, DateTimePredicates.cs, DateTimePredicates.FixedOffset.cs, FixedOffsetText.cs, RegexPredicates.cs, RegexFlags.cs, RegexPatternCache.cs, SelectedValuePredicates.cs, NullBehavior.cs, NullBehaviorScope.cs, PredicateResult.cs, PredicateFamily.cs and AssemblyInfo.cs. I also read PredicateArguments (IsDeferred, TryGet*) in Abstractions to confirm how deferred arguments behave.

Docs I read: the four type-isguid/isnumeric/isurl/isdatetimeoffset pages, datetime-isintimewindow.md, regex-ismatch.md, selectedvalue-create.md, and lines 25-64 of predicates/README.md (null and fault contract table, NotX twins). I did not read ADR-0001, 0002, 0005 or 0006 in full. I relied on the CLAUDE.md summary and on the README contract table for the fault, timeout and cancellation rules. I did not read the other datetime-*, scalar-* or type-isnot* pages, apart from grepping them.

What checks out: null selection gives Unknown by default in every builder, and every NotX twin gives the K3 complement, the null case included. IsNull and IsNotNull are definite. Arguments are read before the selection, so a bad data-source argument faults even when the selection is null. Number, date and offset parsing uses the invariant culture. Clock predicates use TimeProvider.GetUtcNow and compare instants. Reversed bounds are reported at compile time and throw at evaluation.

Three observations are not findings because they do not contradict the docs:
- IsNumeric uses NumberStyles.Float, so leading and trailing whitespace is accepted.
- Uri.TryCreate in IsUrl also trims whitespace.
- The regex delegates ignore the CancellationToken, so a match runs synchronously for up to its 1 s timeout. That timeout surfaces as a fault, which matches the doc.

Two findings rest on BCL behavior that I know but did not run, because the task forbids it: Guid.TryParse trimming whitespace, and Turkish-culture casing for an inline (?i) without CultureInvariant. A one-line test confirms either one.

findings.title: Regex built without CultureInvariant: an inline (?i) depends on the culture of whichever thread first compiled it
findings.summary: RegexOptions.CultureInvariant is added only when the rule sets the 'i' flag. A pattern that turns on case-insensitivity inline with (?i), which regex-ismatch.md documents as a supported way to ignore case, is compiled under CultureInfo.CurrentCulture. The compiled Regex is then cached process-wide (RegexPatternCache.Get, keyed on pattern and options only), so the culture of the first thread that compiles the pattern fixes the answer for every later evaluation.
findings.failure_scenario: The host runs under tr-TR. The rule is `codeIsMatch(pattern: "(?i)^id$")` and the selected value is "ID". With Turkish casing, 'i' and 'I' are not case-equivalent, so the answer is False. On an en-US thread the same rule gives True. If a tr-TR request compiles the pattern first, every later en-US request also gets False from the cache.
findings.expected_behavior: Always add RegexOptions.CultureInvariant, whatever the flags are, so the host culture never changes a match. This is what the predicates README promises for all families.
findings.evidence:
The code path is as claimed.

- src/TruthWeaver.Predicates/RegexFlags.cs:35 adds CultureInvariant only inside the 'i' case. Flags "", "m", "s", "n" and "x" never set it.
- src/TruthWeaver.Predicates/RegexPatternCache.cs:54 builds `new Regex(pattern, options, timeout)` with only those options. Validate (line 37) does the same.
- The cache key at line 47 is (pattern, options) with no culture. The first Regex built for a pair is therefore reused by every later thread, whatever its culture.
- The only other CultureInvariant uses in src are GeneratedRegex attributes and tool code. None cover rule-supplied patterns.

Without CultureInvariant, the Regex parser uses CultureInfo.CurrentCulture when it builds case-equivalence data. An inline (?i) in the pattern triggers this even though RegexOptions.IgnoreCase is not set. .NET 7 and later special-case tr/az casing, where I and i are not equivalent. So `(?i)^id$` against "ID" can be False on a tr-TR thread and True on en-US. The cache then fixes the first answer for every later evaluation of that pattern.

I traced the code and the cache. I did not run it under tr-TR. The Turkish case-folding behavior of .NET's regex parser is from my knowledge of the runtime.

The severity is lower than "high" for two reasons. The trigger needs a host with a Turkish or Azeri culture on the compiling thread, or mixed cultures across threads.
