It also needs a pattern with an inline (?i) and the letters i or I, and it gives a wrong match rather than a crash. The effect is still real: it is non-deterministic and the cache makes it persist. The fix is to always OR RegexOptions.CultureInvariant, for example at the point where RegexPredicates.cs:201 and :218 hand over the parsed options. The same applies when the flags are empty.

findings.title: IsGuid accepts surrounding whitespace, but the doc says it does not trim
findings.summary: GuidTest calls Guid.TryParse, and Guid.TryParse trims leading and trailing whitespace before it parses. type-isguid.md and type-isnotguid.md both state 'The text must be a whole GUID. This predicate does not trim surrounding spaces.' Code and the ground-truth doc give different answers. The doc reads as the intended rule (one spelling, no guessing).
findings.failure_scenario: String selector returns "  d3b07384-d9a3-4c1e-8f3b-0a1b2c3d4e5f ". The doc says IsGuid is False and IsNotGuid is True. The code answers IsGuid True and IsNotGuid False. The object-selector overload behaves the same way for a string.
findings.expected_behavior: Reject text with leading or trailing whitespace, for example by checking that the text is unchanged after a trim before calling Guid.TryParse. The alternative is to change both docs to say whitespace is trimmed.
findings.evidence: src/TruthWeaver.Predicates/TypePredicates.cs:659-667 shows GuidTest(string) is just Guid.TryParse(value, out _), with no whitespace check. GuidTest(object) calls it for a string, so both overloads behave the same. IsGuid and IsNotGuid (lines 45, 77, 109, 141) all route through GuidTest. docs/strong-k3/predicates/type-isguid.md:71 and type-isnotguid.md:71 both say "This predicate does not trim surrounding spaces." The .NET Guid parser trims leading and trailing whitespace before it parses. I know this from the BCL implementation and did not run it here. So "  d3b07384-d9a3-4c1e-8f3b-0a1b2c3d4e5f " gives IsGuid=True and IsNotGuid=False. The doc says False and True. The code and the ground-truth doc disagree. The impact is small: it is a lenient accept of padded GUID text, not a crash or a wrong K3 truth table. I rate it medium.

findings.title: Literal regex pattern is checked with no options when the flags come from a data source, so a valid rule fails to compile
findings.summary: ValidateArguments reads the flags with TryGetString. An omitted flags argument is filled with its default "", so a missing flags value at compile time means it is deferred to a data source. In that case `options` stays RegexOptions.None and the literal pattern is still validated with Cache.Validate. regex-ismatch.md says a data-source flags value is checked at evaluation and that a pattern valid only with 'x' compiles. The validator should skip the pattern check when args.IsDeferred("flags").
findings.failure_scenario: Rule: `codeIsMatch(pattern: "^a+ # one or more (a's", flags: from("request", "$.flags"))`, where the data source supplies "x". Under 'x' the '(' is inside a comment and the pattern is valid. Under None the paren is unbalanced, so the compiler reports TRE0026 and rejects a rule that would evaluate correctly.
findings.expected_behavior: When flags is deferred, do not validate the literal pattern at compile time. Leave the check to evaluation, where the real options are known.

findings.title: Calendar predicates fault on a valid instant near DateTimeOffset.MinValue/MaxValue, including default(DateTimeOffset)
findings.summary: BindTimeWindow (line 344), BindMonths (line 510) and BindDays (line 571) call instant.ToOffset(offset). ToOffset throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException when the local clock time would fall outside the DateTime range. A selected instant that is valid but near either end of the range therefore gives Unknown plus a Fault, not a definite answer. It also counts toward FaultBudget. No doc mentions this edge.
findings.failure_scenario: The selector returns a non-nullable DateTimeOffset field that was never set, so the value is default(DateTimeOffset), 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z. The rule is `isWeekday(days: ["Monday"], offset: "-05:00")`. ToOffset(-5h) throws, so the answer is Unknown with one fault. With offset "Z" the same value answers definitely, and DateTimeOffset.MaxValue with a positive offset fails the same way.
findings.expected_behavior: Compute the local calendar fields from UtcDateTime.Ticks + offset.Ticks without building a DateTimeOffset. Or clamp the value and document the behavior, so that every representable instant gets a definite True or False.

findings.title: FixedOffsetText regexes use '$', so a trailing newline is accepted
findings.summary: OffsetPattern, TimeOfDayPattern and DurationPattern anchor with '$'. Without Multiline, '$' also matches before a final '\n'. The class remarks say only one spelling per value is accepted, and the docs list exact forms.
findings.failure_scenario: A YAML or JSON rule gives `offset: "+05:30\n"` or `start: "09:00\n"`. The compile-time validator accepts it with no TRE0026, and evaluation uses +05:30 or 09:00. A data-source value with a stray newline is accepted the same way. The documented grammar should reject both.
findings.expected_behavior: Anchor with \z, or use RegexOptions.NonBacktracking with \z, so only the exact documented form matches.

findings.title: Factories do not validate the NullBehavior value; an undefined value silently acts as Unknown
findings.summary: Resolve returns any value other than Default unchanged. ForNullAsync (PredicateResult.cs:31) then treats every value except False as Unknown. NullBehaviorScope.Begin rejects bad values, but the factory parameter that the doc says 'always wins' gets no check at all.
findings.failure_scenario: A host passes `(NullBehavior)3`, for example a value cast from configuration and mistyped. The intent was False, but registration succeeds and every null selection answers Unknown, with no error at registration time.
findings.expected_behavior: Resolve, or each factory, throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for a value that is not Unknown, False or Default. This matches the validation in NullBehaviorScope.Open.

findings.title: Disposing scopes out of order can bring back a disposed NullBehaviorScope
findings.summary: Dispose sets Current.Value to this.parent without checking that this scope is the current one. If an outer scope is disposed before an inner one, disposing the inner scope later restores the outer scope, which is already disposed, as the ambient default.
findings.failure_scenario: `var a = NullBehaviorScope.Begin(NullBehavior.False); var b = NullBehaviorScope.Begin(PredicateFamily.Type, NullBehavior.Unknown); a.Dispose(); b.Dispose();` Both scopes are now disposed, but Current is `a`. Every later factory call on that flow resolves Default to False, not to the documented no-scope default, Unknown.
findings.expected_behavior: Dispose only restores the parent when this scope is Current.Value, or unwinds past disposed ancestors. An out-of-order dispose should not leave a disposed scope in effect.

reviewers.label: F8 Predicate+DataSource concepts
reviewers.coverage:
I read every file in scope in full: src/TruthWeaver/Registry (CollectionBinding, Element, ICollectionBinding, LazyElementDataSource, PredicateAudit, PredicateDescriptor, PredicateRegistry, PredicateRegistryBuilder); IDataSource.cs and DataSources.cs; DataSourceDeclarations.cs; DataSourceExtensions.cs; src/TruthWeaver.DataSources.Json (JsonDataSource, JsonPaths, JsonQueryValidator); YamlDataSource.cs; src/TruthWeaver.Generators (PredicateMethodReader, RegisterEmitter, PredicateRegistrationGenerator, PredicateAttributeSource, GeneratorDiagnostics, README).

findings.title: TryGetAsync/GetAsync classify an object, array or null match as SourceError; a variable classifies the same match as TypeMismatch
findings.summary: TryGetAsync maps every DataQueryResult error kind, UnsupportedType included, to VariableFailureKind.SourceError. The evaluator maps UnsupportedType to TypeMismatch (Evaluator.cs:801-804). docs/data-sources.md:246-252 says GetAsync 'converts like a variable would' and lists TypeMismatch as a failure kind. So the eager read and the deferred read disagree on the same data.
findings.failure_scenario: JsonDataSource.Parse("{\"limits\":{\"age\":null}}").TryGetAsync<long>("$.limits.age") returns FailureKind = SourceError. A rule term ageAtLeast(min: from("cfg", "$.limits.age")) against the same document records a TypeMismatch fault. Host code that branches on FailureKind (for example, retry on SourceError) retries a data problem that can never succeed.
findings.expected_behavior: Map UnsupportedType to TypeMismatch in TryGetAsync, as Evaluator.QuerySourceUncachedAsync does, so both paths report one kind.

findings.title: JsonDataSource throws instead of converting when a node holds a CLR value (Guid, DateTimeOffset, char, NaN)
findings.summary: TryConvert calls value.GetValue<string>() whenever GetValueKind() is String. A JsonValue built from a CLR Guid or DateTimeOffset (JsonValue.Create or the JsonNode implicit conversions) reports kind String, but GetValue<string>() throws InvalidOperationException for it. A CLR double NaN makes ToJsonString() at line 185 throw. The number branch is written to avoid this problem (comment at lines 177-178), but the string branch is not. ADR-0006 decision 9 says the source reports such failures as data, not as exceptions. (PLAUSIBLE: depends on the System.Text.Json JsonValuePrimitive<T>.TryGetValue behavior.)
findings.failure_scenario: JsonDataSource.Create(new JsonObject { ["id"] = Guid.NewGuid() }) and a rule isOwner(id: from("doc", "$.id")) with a Guid argument. QueryAsync throws InvalidOperationException, and the evaluator backstop records a SourceError fault (term is Unknown). The docs say a matched string converts to a Guid. YamlDataSource never hits this because it builds string-backed values.
findings.expected_behavior: Read a String-kind value through TryGetValue<string> and fall back to the node's JSON text (ToJsonString, unquoted), or return an UnsupportedType or SourceFailure result. Do not throw.

findings.title: Registry and generator accept predicate and collection names that rule text cannot express, so a JSON-compiled rule prints unparsable DSL
findings.summary: AddDescriptor rejects only reserved words and case duplicates. It does not check that the name is a DSL identifier (Lexer.cs:33-40: a letter or '_' first, then letters, digits and '_'). Empty names and names with '-', '.' or spaces register. TreeFormatReader.ReadTerm accepts any string, and CanonicalPrinter writes the name verbatim. AddCollection (line 89) has no reserved-word or identifier check at all. The generator (PredicateRegistrationGenerator.Distinct) checks only reserved words.
findings.failure_scenario: Register a predicate named "has-role". CompileJson({"predicate":"has-role"}) succeeds. CompiledRule.PrintRuleText() emits has-role, which re-parses as has - role and fails. RuleFormat promises that all three formats round-trip without loss. AddCollection("and", ...) registers a binding that no FORALL(x IN and, ...) can name, with no error.
findings.expected_behavior: Reject a predicate or collection name that is not a DSL identifier, or is reserved, at registration (ArgumentException), and add a matching generator diagnostic.

findings.title: A quantifier variable that shadows a declared source keeps the hidden source's validator for element queries
findings.summary: DeclareElementSource copies the outer declarations and then calls declared.Add(variable), which keeps an existing validator. At evaluation, WithElementSource (line 268-276) makes the element source win over the outer source of the same name. So compile-time syntax checks for from(variable, ...) run in the dialect of a source the body can never reach. The ADR-0010 amendment states both rules (keep the validator, the element wins), and together they contradict ADR-0006 decision 4: a validator checks a query in that source's dialect.
findings.failure_scenario: The outer "user" is declared with JsonQueryValidator.Instance. A collection "orders" has an elementSource that projects to a custom key-value source whose dialect is "total". The rule FORALL(user IN orders, over(limit: from("user", "total"))) fails to compile with TRE0025 (not valid JSONPath), although the query is valid for the source it reaches at evaluation. The reverse case also happens: a query that is malformed for the element source is not flagged because JSONPath accepts it.
findings.expected_behavior: Inside the body, declare the variable without a validator (replace the outer entry), or report a shadowing diagnostic when the variable name equals a declared source.

findings.title: TryGetAsync does not catch a source exception, so its 'result instead of throwing' contract fails for a thrown backend failure
findings.summary: TryGetAsync awaits source.QueryAsync with no try/catch. ADR-0006 decision 9 and docs/data-sources.md:356-357 let a source throw, and the evaluator treats a throw as a SourceError (Evaluator.cs:767-784). The docs (lines 246-253) say GetAsync throws InvalidOperationException when the source fails, and that TryGetAsync returns a SourceError result instead of throwing.
findings.failure_scenario: An IDataSource over an HTTP config service throws HttpRequestException. TryGetAsync<long>("$.limits.age") propagates HttpRequestException instead of returning FailureKind = SourceError. GetAsync throws HttpRequestException, not the documented InvalidOperationException. The same source used as a rule variable gives Unknown plus a SourceError fault.
findings.expected_behavior: Catch non-cancellation exceptions (same filter as the evaluator) and return DataReadResult.Failure(SourceError, ...) with no data in the message.

findings.title: The generator does not detect argument names that differ only in case; Register then throws at run time
findings.summary: C# parameter names are case-sensitive, so a [Predicate] method can declare string role and string Role. The generator emits both as arguments with no diagnostic. PredicateRegistryBuilder.RejectCaseVariantArguments then throws ArgumentException when Register runs. GeneratorDiagnostics.cs:6-7 and docs/predicate-source-generator.md:132 say every problem is a build error and never reaches run time.
findings.failure_scenario: [Predicate("hasRole","Has role","...")] static TruthValue HasRole(User u, string role, string Role = "x"). The project builds. OrderPredicates.Register(builder) throws ArgumentException at host startup.
findings.expected_behavior: Add a TWG diagnostic for argument names that collide when case is ignored, and register no method that has one.

findings.title: Lambda registration accepts a null delegate and fails on every evaluation instead of at registration
findings.summary: Add(schema, evaluate) does not null-check schema or evaluate. A null evaluate gives a descriptor with Evaluate and ImplementationType both null. Evaluator.cs:634-636 then goes to InvokeClassBasedAsync and calls services.GetService(null!). That throws, and the throw becomes a fault on every evaluation. A null schema throws NullReferenceException instead of the documented ArgumentException.
findings.failure_scenario: builder.Add(schema, null!) (for example, from a factory that returns null) builds without error. Every term of that predicate evaluates Unknown with an ArgumentNullException fault. The programming error never surfaces at startup.
findings.expected_behavior: ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(schema) and ThrowIfNull(evaluate) in Add, like AddCollection does.

findings.title: The element projector runs once per distinct query, not once per element as ADR-0010 states
findings.summary: LazyElementDataSource calls projector(item) on every QueryAsync and ScopeAsync. The ADR-0010 amendment says 'the delegate runs at the first query of that element'. The evaluator memoizes per (scope, reference), so each distinct query of one element builds a new source.
findings.failure_scenario: elementSource = item => JsonDataSource.Create(JsonSerializer.SerializeToNode(item)), and a body with three different from(line, ...) references over 10,000 lines. The code serializes 30,000 times instead of 10,000. A projector with side effects or non-deterministic output gives different terms of one element different views of the element.
findings.expected_behavior: Cache the projected source (or the projection exception) in LazyElementDataSource after the first call.

findings.title: Outer data sources are queried again for each quantifier element, against ADR-0006 decision 11
findings.summary: WithElementSource passes outer sources unchanged into each nested evaluator, but the answer memo key is (memoScope, reference) (Evaluator.cs:742), and memoScope differs per element. An outer from("cfg", "$.limit") inside a body is queried once per element. ADR-0006 decision 11 says each (source, query) pair is queried at most once within one evaluation.
findings.failure_scenario: FORALL(line IN lines, under(max: from("cfg", "$.limit"))) over 500 lines, with a live config source. That makes 500 backend calls. If the value changes during the evaluation, line 1 and line 400 are checked against different limits within one evaluation.
findings.expected_behavior: Memoize references to sources that the element binding does not shadow at the outer scope, or amend ADR-0006 decision 11 to state the per-element scope.

findings.title: YAML mapping keys that are not scalars all collapse to an empty-string key, and the data is silently overwritten
findings.summary: The comment says a non-scalar key 'is read as its text', but the code maps every sequence or mapping key to string.Empty. YamlDotNet compares keys structurally, so it does not report [a] and [b] as duplicates. Both become "" and the later value replaces the earlier one with no error. The same data as JSON cannot be expressed this way, and Parse and TryParse report duplicate keys as errors only for scalar keys.
findings.failure_scenario:
YAML '? [a]
: 1
? [b]
: 2
' parses without error. $[''] matches 2, and the first entry is lost. TryParse returns true.
findings.expected_behavior: Reject a non-scalar mapping key with a YamlException (positioned, no content), consistent with the duplicate-key rule.

findings.title: The docs name a fault kind 'UnsupportedType' that faults never carry
findings.summary: The Missing/null/empty table says a JSON null match records a fault of kind 'UnsupportedType for null'. VariableFailureKind has no UnsupportedType member. The evaluator maps a DataQueryErrorKind.UnsupportedType result to VariableFailureKind.TypeMismatch (Evaluator.cs:801-804), so the fault kind is TypeMismatch for a null, an object or an array. The docs side looks wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: A host follows the table and filters faults for an 'UnsupportedType' kind to detect null data. It finds none: the fault's Kind is TypeMismatch, and 'UnsupportedType' appears only inside the message text.
findings.expected_behavior: The row should say the fault is TypeMismatch, and that the message names the source's UnsupportedType error.

reviewers.label: F9 Policies
reviewers.coverage:
I fully read every non-generated file in src/TruthWeaver.Policies: CombiningAlgorithm.cs, Policy{TContext}.cs, PolicyDecision.cs, PolicyEffect.cs, PolicyOutcome.cs, PolicyResult.cs, PolicySet{TContext}.cs and README.md. I also read docs/policies.md, ADR-0015 and the fault-budget section of ADR-0002. For the shared-state dependencies I read CompiledRule.Evaluation.cs, EvaluationState.cs, EvaluationOptions.cs (header), parts of CompiledRule.cs and NodeShape.cs, Evaluator.cs (lines 25-160 and 420-670) and CollectionBinding.cs (lines 80-200).

I checked the combining table against ADR-0015, docs/policies.md, the README and the enum docs for every mix of True, False, Unknown and faulted members. In Combine, Decides, AppliesAsync and the set-target handling, DenyOverrides, PermitOverrides and FirstApplicable match the documented table. The policy-applicability K3 AND (target, condition) matches the docs. The Unknown set target turns any outcome other than NotApplicable into Indeterminate. NotApplicable maps to False and only Permit is satisfied, so results fail closed. Early stopping does not change the outcome when no fault budget or element bound is set.

The findings come from the shared EvaluationState (fault filtering, budget, element bound, memo, trace) and from one core-evaluator abort defect that the set makes reachable. I did not read ADR-0001, ADR-0005, ADR-0006 or the docs/strong-k3 pages in full, because the policy semantics are defined in ADR-0015. I did not read the rest of Evaluator.cs or the tests. I did not check whether definitions are inlined before CollectTermIdentities runs.

findings.title: Collection faults are dropped from PolicyDecision.Decision.Faults
findings.summary: RunAsync keeps only the faults whose Term is in rule.TermIdentities. CollectTermIdentities (src/TruthWeaver/Evaluation/CompiledRule.cs:147-167) adds TermExpression identities only, and ExpressionShape gives a quantifier its body as the only operand. A quantifier fault is recorded against new TermIdentity(collectionName, []) (CollectionBinding.cs:111 for a throwing selector, :175 for MaxElementEvaluations, Evaluator.cs:438 for an unregistered collection). That identity is never in the set, so the filter drops the fault. This breaks ADR-0001 (an Unknown carries its Fault) and the PolicyDecision doc ('Its faults are those of every rule that was evaluated').
findings.failure_scenario: A deny policy has condition `EXISTS(o IN orders, isOverdue)` and the `orders` selector throws. The policy is Unknown, so DenyOverrides answers Indeterminate, but PolicyDecision.Decision.Faults is empty. The host cannot see why access was refused. Calling the same CompiledRule directly with EvaluateAsync reports the fault, so the two layers disagree.
findings.expected_behavior: Every fault recorded while a rule of the set ran, including quantifier and collection faults, appears in PolicyDecision.Decision.Faults. For example, filter by the faults this rule added (state.Faults count before and after), plus the memo-shared term faults.
findings.evidence: The fault is dropped by the filter at src/TruthWeaver.Policies/PolicySet{TContext}.cs:171-174. RunAsync calls rule.EvaluateAsync with the shared EvaluationState. Evaluator.cs:72-74 builds the Decision from this.state.Faults, so the Decision does contain collection faults. RunAsync then keeps only faults where ownTerms.Contains(fault.Term). ownTerms is rule.TermIdentities. CollectTermIdentities (CompiledRule.cs:147-167) adds an identity only for TermExpression nodes and otherwise walks ExpressionShape.Of(node).Operands. NodeShape.cs:67 gives a QuantifierExpression the single operand q.Body, so only the body's terms are collected. Collection faults use new TermIdentity(collectionName, []). It is created at CollectionBinding.cs:111 (throwing selector), CollectionBinding.cs:175 (MaxElementEvaluations) and Evaluator.cs:438 (unregistered collection). None of these is a TermExpression identity in the tree, so they are never in the set and the filter drops them. A policy condition `EXISTS(o IN orders, isOverdue)` whose `orders` selector throws therefore gives Unknown and an Indeterminate outcome with an empty PolicyDecision.Decision.Faults. I traced this by reading the code and did not run it. Severity is lowered from high to medium. The outcome stays correct and fail-closed. Only the fault diagnostics are lost, and the Policies layer then disagrees with a direct CompiledRule.EvaluateAsync call.

findings.title: Shared fault budget makes the overriding outcome depend on priority, against ADR-0015 section 4
findings.summary: ADR-0015 section 4 and docs/policies.md say that under DenyOverrides and PermitOverrides the outcome does not depend on order, and that a priority never changes an outcome. The set uses one EvaluationState, so FaultBudget and MaxElementEvaluations are spent across policies in priority order. After an earlier policy spends the budget, every later rule's root returns Unknown (Evaluator.cs:140). Reordering the policies then changes the outcome. The docs describe the shared budget but keep the order-independence claim. One of the two statements is wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: DenyOverrides with FaultBudget = 1. Permit policy P (priority 10) has a condition that faults. Deny policy D (priority 0) has `isBlocked`, which is True. Order P then D: P is Unknown and the budget aborts, so D is Unknown and the outcome is Indeterminate. Swap the priorities: D is True, the walk stops, and the outcome is Deny. Both results fail closed, but the documented invariant does not hold.
findings.expected_behavior: Either the docs and ADR say that a fault budget or element bound can make the outcome depend on priority, or the set gives each rule its own budget accounting, so the order-independence claim holds.
findings.evidence: I traced the path in the code. src/TruthWeaver.Policies/PolicySet{TContext}.cs:101 creates one EvaluationState for the whole set. Policies run in priority order (:59 sorts, :123 loops). Each rule is evaluated through rule.EvaluateAsync(context, sharedState, ...) (:171). Evaluator.cs:649-659 sets state.Aborted = true once state.Faults.Count >= FaultBudget. The state is shared, so the flag stays set for later rules. Evaluator.cs:140-148 then returns Unknown for the root node of every later rule without running it. Concrete case: DenyOverrides, FaultBudget = 1, permit policy P (priority 10) with a faulting condition, deny policy D (priority 0) with isBlocked = True. P runs first, faults and sets Aborted. D then returns Unknown, so Decides() never fires and Combine() reaches Has(Deny, Unknown) and returns Indeterminate. With D at the higher priority, D evaluates True, Decides() stops the walk, and the outcome is Deny. The outcome therefore depends on priority. docs/policies.md:62 says that under the overriding algorithms the outcome does not depend on the order. docs/policies.md:70 states the whole-set fault budget in the same page, so the two statements contradict each other. I did not open ADR-0015 section 4. The same shared-state flag applies to MaxElementEvaluations, because that limit also sets Aborted. Both results fail closed (Indeterminate maps to Unknown, and IsSatisfied is fail-closed), so this is an inconsistency between documented behaviour and a bounded edge case. It is not a security hole.

findings.title: A fault-budget abort in an AND/OR chain drops the skipped operands, so a policy can be definitely False or True
findings.summary: In EvalChainAsync, an operand skipped because state.Aborted is set adds nothing to the accumulator. The chain keeps the fold of the operands before the abort. When the operand that faulted is wrapped in an inspection (IsTrue/IsFalse/IsKnown/IsUnknown), it gives a definite value. The chain can then return False for OR (or True for AND) while a later operand was never evaluated. In K3, an unevaluated operand must count as Unknown. A policy set makes this easier to trigger, because faults from earlier rules count against the same budget. This is core evaluator code outside the Policies slice. It is reported here because it causes a silent permit through a set.
findings.failure_scenario: DenyOverrides with FaultBudget = 1. Permit policy `staff` is True. Deny policy has condition `IsTrue(isSanctioned) OR isBlocked`. isSanctioned throws: IsTrue gives False, the budget aborts, and isBlocked is skipped. The OR returns a definite False, so the deny does not apply and the set answers Permit. isBlocked, which would have been True, never ran.
findings.expected_behavior: An operand skipped because of an abort folds as Unknown, so the chain is Unknown. The deny policy is then Unknown and DenyOverrides answers Indeterminate.
findings.evidence:
Traced in src/TruthWeaver/Evaluation/Evaluator.cs. For OR(IsTrue(isSanctioned), isBlocked) with FaultBudget=1:
1. EvalChainAsync (474-509) starts with accumulator=False (the OR identity). Operand 1 is an InspectionExpression, so EvalAsync (215-218) runs it.
2. isSanctioned throws. InvokeCoreAsync (638-646) calls RecordFault and returns Unknown. RecordFault (650-661) sets state.Aborted = true because Faults.Count >= budget.
3. K3Logic.Inspect(IsTrue, Unknown) returns False, a definite value. Line 498 folds it, so accumulator = False. False is not the OR stop value (True), so stop stays false.
4. For operand 2, line 488 (`stop || this.state.Aborted`) is true. The chain only records a NotEvaluated trace node and `continue`s. It never calls combine with Unknown. The accumulator stays False.
5. The chain returns a definite False at line 505, with no Unknown. Nothing else reads Aborted: it is used only at Evaluator.cs:140/488/659 and CollectionBinding, and it never reaches the result. A caller sees False, and the only sign is the recorded Fault.
EvalAsync (140-148) correctly returns Unknown for a skipped single node, but EvalChainAsync bypasses it. The docs say the same: docs/diagnostics.md:170 says terms not yet run are Unknown in the trace, so the result is usually Unknown. The xmldoc at 467-472 claims stopping never changes the result, which holds only for short-circuit stops, not abort skips.
The scenario works for AND with IsFalse/IsUnknown as well. Without an inspection wrapper, the faulting term is Unknown and the fold usually stays Unknown, so the bug needs an external operator (IsTrue/IsFalse/IsKnown/IsUnknown) to turn Unknown into a definite value.
I did not trace the policy-set layer. The core evaluator defect is confirmed, and the DenyOverrides outcome (Permit instead of Indeterminate) follows if the policy condition is evaluated through this chain and its result is used as-is.
Severity: high. Fail-open is only possible with FaultBudget set and a faulting term wrapped in an inspection. The abort is a deliberate opt-in. The result is a wrong definite value for an authorization decision.

findings.title: Term memo is shared across rules compiled with different registries
findings.summary: The shared EvaluationState keys Memo by (scope, TermIdentity) and CollectionMaterializations by (scope, collection name). Neither key includes the registry. PolicySet accepts rules from any compiler and does not check that they share one PredicateRegistry. docs/policies.md states this ('whichever rule compiled them'). The result is that one rule's answer can stand in for a different predicate or a different compile mode.
findings.failure_scenario: The set target is compiled in Lenient mode against a registry where `isAdmin` is missing. It memoizes Unknown for isAdmin and records a fault. A permit policy compiled in Strict mode with a registered `isAdmin` then hits the memo: the real predicate never runs, the policy is Unknown, and the set is Indeterminate. In the same way, two registries that bind the name `isAdmin` to different implementations reuse whichever ran first.
findings.expected_behavior: Either the set rejects rules whose registries differ (or are incompatible), or the memo key includes the registry identity, so each rule evaluates its own predicates.

findings.title: MaxElementEvaluations is a whole-set bound but is documented as per evaluation
findings.summary: state.ElementEvaluations lives in the shared EvaluationState, so the 10,000 default bound (EvaluationOptions.cs:24-31, 'in one evaluation') is spent across all rules of the set. docs/policies.md and ADR-0015 say only the fault budget becomes a whole-set concept. When the bound is hit, the set aborts and every later rule is Unknown. Because of the first finding, the limit fault is also dropped.
findings.failure_scenario: Three policies each contain `FORALL(l IN lines, ...)` over a 4,000-line order. Each rule alone is under the limit. In the set, the third quantifier exceeds 10,000, the evaluation aborts, the third and later policies are Unknown, and the outcome is Indeterminate with no fault in PolicyDecision.Decision.Faults.
findings.expected_behavior: docs/policies.md says the element bound is shared across the set, or the set accounts for the element bound per rule.

findings.title: IncludeTrace collects a trace that PolicyDecision never returns
findings.summary: The shared state collects trace entries when options.IncludeTrace is true. Each rule's Decision copies the full trace so far, so the cost grows quadratically with the number of rules. Build then creates a new Decision with no trace, so the caller gets nothing for this cost. No doc says what IncludeTrace does for a set.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes EvaluationOptions(IncludeTrace: true) to a 50-policy set to debug a denial. Every rule allocates a copy of the growing trace, and PolicyDecision.Decision.Trace is still null.
findings.expected_behavior: Either the set's decision carries the trace (or each policy's trace), or the docs say that IncludeTrace has no effect on a set and the set does not collect one.

reviewers.label: T2 Surfaces
reviewers.coverage: I read in full: Json/JsonTreeParser.cs, JsonNodeCursor.cs, JsonNodeWriter.cs, JsonTreePrinter.cs, JsonSpanLocator.cs, DecisionJsonReader.cs, TraceTextRedaction.cs, rule-tree.schema.json; Yaml/YamlTreeParser.cs, YamlNodeCursor.cs, YamlNodeWriter.cs, YamlTreePrinter.cs, YamlRuleDefinitions.cs, YamlRuleExtensions.cs, RuleFormatExtensions.cs; Printing/CanonicalPrinter.cs, RuleText.cs, RuleTextOptions.cs, OperatorStyle.cs, TreeFormatEmitter.cs, EquationPrinter.cs, EquationTokens.cs, LatexText.cs, TypstText.cs, AsciiMathText.cs, MathMlText.cs, HtmlPrinter.cs, HtmlText.cs, DotPrinter.cs, RuleRenderTree.cs, NodeStyle.cs, TruthTablePrinter.cs (lines 40-393); MermaidTreePrinter.cs lines 110-331; Building/RuleBuilder.cs lines 700-1221; Diagnostics/DiagnosticFormatter.cs, NameSuggester.cs, SourceSpan.cs. I read these as context, outside the slice: OperatorDefinitions.cs, TreeFormatOpNames.cs, Lexer.ReadString, RuleNodeCompiler duplicate-argument code, CollectionBinding quantifier trace, Evaluator quantifier/chain, LiteralValue, LiteralKind, the TreeFormatReader head (no depth or cycle guard found by grep), the ADR-0005 alias decisions, and docs syntax.md and diagnostics.md lines about duplicates. Files I did not read or only skimmed: RuleBuilder.cs lines 1-700 (factory methods); MermaidTreePrinter.cs lines 1-110; MermaidOptions/Builder/Palette; PlainTextTreePrinter.cs; ConstantFormat.cs; ConstantStyle, AsciiText, EquationOptions/Legend, GroupingStyle, DotOptions, HtmlOptions, TruthTableOptions, RenderNode/State, ITreeWriter; DecisionJsonWriter.cs and DecisionJsonNames.cs (only via snippets); decision-record.schema.json; Building/Arg.cs, DataReadResult.cs, DataSourceExtensions.cs, RuleDefinition.cs; Diagnostics/Diagnostic.cs (partial), DiagnosticCodes.cs; Yaml/RuleConversionResult.cs, AssemblyInfo.cs. Some points rest on known BCL or YamlDotNet behavior that I did not run: JsonElement.TryGetProperty returns the last duplicate (the comment at JsonSpanLocator.cs:100 agrees); JsonDocument's default MaxDepth is 64; JsonDocument.Parse(string) throws ArgumentException on a lone surrogate; Utf8JsonWriter rejects NaN; YamlDotNet builds cyclic graphs for self-aliases (the repo's YamlDataSourceTests agree). I checked operator names and labels across the schema, OperatorDefinitions, CanonicalPrinter, EquationTokens and RuleRenderTree and found them consistent. The schema op patterns match TreeFormatOpNames, including the xnor/iff aliases (ADR-0005 decision 5). Canonical parenthesization and escaping matched the Lexer.

findings.title: YAML self-referencing alias or very deep nesting overflows the stack while parsing a rule
findings.summary: YamlStream.Load resolves aliases into shared node references, so an anchor that is aliased inside its own body gives a cyclic YamlNode graph. YamlNodeCursor (lines 170-189) hands child nodes straight to TreeFormatReader.ReadNode, which recurses with no cycle check and no depth limit. JSON is capped at depth 64 by JsonDocument, but nothing bounds YAML nesting. The repository already knows the cycle exists: YamlDataSource.ToJson keeps an ancestor set for exactly this case, and YamlDataSourceTests pins `a: &x [*x]`.
findings.failure_scenario:
`compiler.CompileYaml("&r
op: not
operands: [*r]
")`, or a 50,000-level `{op: not, operands: [...]}` chain, recurses until a StackOverflowException. That exception cannot be caught, so one untrusted rule document kills the host process. The documented contract is a MalformedTree diagnostic.
findings.expected_behavior: Detect alias cycles by reference (as YamlDataSource does) and enforce a nesting limit in line with JSON's, so both produce a diagnostic.
findings.evidence:
The reader has no cycle or depth guard.

Trace for `&r\nop: not\noperands: [*r]`:
- YamlTreeParser.Parse (src/TruthWeaver.Yaml/YamlTreeParser.cs:31, 57) calls `stream.Load` and passes `Documents[0].RootNode` to `TreeFormatReader.Read(new YamlNodeCursor(node), ...)`.
- `Read` (src/TruthWeaver/Parsing/TreeFormatReader.cs:68) calls `ReadNode` (:149), which calls `ReadNodeCore`, then `ReadOperator`, then `ReadNode` on each operand. This is plain recursion.
- A grep of src for `EnsureSufficientExecutionStack`, `TryEnsureSufficientExecutionStack` and `MaxNesting` returns nothing.
- The only depth limit is `CompilerOptions.MaxDepth` (default 32), checked in RuleNodeCompiler.cs:226. That runs after the raw tree is built, so it cannot stop the read.

Cycle:
- YamlDotNet registers an anchor before it loads the node's children, so `*r` inside `&r` resolves to the same node object. This is based on my recollection of YamlDotNet, not a trace of its source.
- The repo's own tests agree: YamlDataSourceTests.cs:179 and :189 pin `a: &x [*x]` as a self-referencing alias that must be rejected, and the cursor code has a branch for "an alias" nodes.
- I did not run the sample. The reader recurses forever on it, so it would end in a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught.

Deep nesting without aliases:
- There is no limit on YAML depth, and the JSON path is bounded by `JsonDocument`.
- Very deep YAML recurses without bound in `ReadNode`, and probably also inside YamlDotNet's own loader. I did not trace the second part.

Impact: a single untrusted YAML rule document kills the host process. The documented contract is a MalformedTree diagnostic.

Severity: critical is defensible because the process crashes, but it needs the attacker to supply the YAML rule text. I rate it high.

findings.title: YAML anchors and aliases allow exponential rule expansion before any size limit runs
findings.summary: Every alias is followed as a full copy of its anchor. TreeFormatReader builds one RuleNode and one path string per visit before RuleNodeCompiler applies MaxDepth or MaxNodeCount. The DSL and JSON `let`/definitions route is bounded by MaxDefinitionDepth (ADR-0008 decision 6), but YAML aliases bypass that guard.
findings.failure_scenario: A document of about 1 KB with nine levels, each `{op: and, operands: [*prev, *prev, ...10 times]}`, is 9 deep (under MaxDepth 32) but expands to 10^9 RuleNodes while parsing. CompileYaml runs out of memory or hangs instead of returning MaxNodeCount/MaxDepth diagnostics.
findings.expected_behavior: Reject aliases in rule trees, or count expanded nodes while reading and stop with a diagnostic at MaxNodeCount.
findings.evidence: Traced path. src/TruthWeaver.Yaml/YamlRuleExtensions.cs:24 calls YamlTreeParser.Parse(yaml). YamlTreeParser.cs:27-32 runs YamlStream.Load, which resolves each alias to the same anchored YamlNode instance, so the model is a DAG and is small. YamlTreeParser.cs:57 and :68 pass the root to TreeFormatReader.Read(new YamlNodeCursor(node)). YamlNodeCursor.ElementsOf (YamlNodeCursor.cs:170-176) and MembersOf (:178-190) yield one cursor per child edge and never track visited nodes. An aliased child is therefore walked in full on every reference, and the reader builds a RuleNode and a path string per visit. TreeFormatReader.cs has no depth or count limit: grep for Depth/Count/Limit/Max finds only operand-arity checks. MaxDepth and MaxNodeCount are enforced only in RuleNodeCompiler (lines 206-233), which runs after the whole raw tree exists. Nothing else in src/TruthWeaver.Yaml checks input length or alias use. With 10 references per level and 9 levels, the raw tree has about 10^9 nodes while the YAML document nests only 9 deep, so the depth cap would not reject it. I did not run it. Memory or time is exhausted before TRE0009/TRE0010 can be returned. This is a billion-laughs style denial of service on untrusted YAML. It is not a correctness problem, and it needs the caller to compile untrusted YAML. I assign high because it is unbounded and easy to trigger. Medium would also be defensible.

findings.title: JSON rule trees silently accept duplicate keys (last wins) while YAML rejects them
findings.summary: JsonDocument.Parse uses the default options, so duplicate properties are allowed. JsonNodeCursor.TryGetChild (JsonNodeCursor.cs:79) resolves to the last occurrence, as JsonSpanLocator.cs:100 also notes. CheckKeys only checks each name against the allowed list, so it never flags a repeat. YAML fails the same document with MalformedTree, and DecisionJsonReader sets AllowDuplicateProperties=false. docs/strong-k3/specification/syntax.md says a node has only the keys of its kind, and the TRE0032 rule says 'no occurrence wins'.
findings.failure_scenario: `{"op":"or","op":"and","operands":[...]}` or `{"const":true,"const":false}` compiles from JSON as AND / False. A reviewer reading the first key sees OR / True. The same tree in YAML is rejected. For an authorization rule this hides what the rule actually means.
findings.expected_behavior: Parse with AllowDuplicateProperties=false (or detect repeats in CheckKeys) and report MalformedTree, the same as YAML.
findings.evidence:
The JSON path accepts duplicate keys and the last one wins.

1. src/TruthWeaver/Json/JsonTreeParser.cs:34 calls `JsonDocument.Parse(json)` with default options. The only other `AllowDuplicateProperties=false` in the Json folder is DecisionJsonReader.cs:37, so the tree parser does not set it. As far as I recall, the .NET 9+ default allows duplicates. I did not look that up.
2. JsonNodeCursor.cs:79 resolves `TryGetChild` through `element.TryGetProperty`, which returns the last occurrence. JsonSpanLocator.cs:100 says the same.
3. TreeFormatReader.CheckKeys (lines 106-139) only checks that each member name is in the `allowed` list. `{"op":"or","op":"and",...}` passes because both `op` entries are allowed, and nothing checks for a repeat. The node then compiles as AND, because `TryGetChild("op")` returns the last value.
4. `{"const":true,"const":false}` compiles to False the same way.
5. YAML rejects the same document. YamlTreeParser.cs:37 and :99-154 catch the YamlDotNet duplicate-key exception and report it. The test `CompileYaml_DuplicateKeyOutsideArgs_ReportsMalformedTree_Test` (StrictTreeKeysTests.cs:159) covers this.
6. A JSON rule with a repeated predicate argument inside `args` is not flagged either. YAML reports TRE0032 `DuplicateArgument` for that case.

I did not open docs/strong-k3/specification/syntax.md, so the claim about its wording is unchecked. I also did not find a JSON duplicate-key test.

Severity is medium, not high. The author writes the JSON, and the effect is a silent mismatch between what a reviewer reads and what compiles. It is not a crash or an engine-semantics break. It does matter for authorization rules.

findings.title: JSON surface is capped at JsonDocument's default depth of 64; RuleBuilder.Compile throws JsonException
findings.summary: Each tree level costs two JSON levels (object plus operands array), and args and array literals add more. JsonTreeParser.cs:34 and RuleBuilder.Compile both parse with default JsonDocumentOptions (MaxDepth 64), whatever CompilerOptions.MaxDepth is set to. RuleBuilder.Compile does not catch the JsonException.
findings.failure_scenario: With default options, a 32-deep rule (allowed by MaxDepth 32), such as 31 NOTs over `hasAnyRole(roles: ["a"])`, compiles from rule text. Its PrintJson output reaches JSON depth 65: CompileJson reports MalformedTree 'depth exceeds 64' instead of compiling, and the equivalent RuleBuilder.Compile throws JsonException. With MaxDepth raised to 50, a 40-deep rule compiles from text and YAML but never from JSON or the builder, so the round trip breaks.
findings.expected_behavior: Derive the JsonDocument MaxDepth from CompilerOptions.MaxDepth (about 2*MaxDepth plus headroom), let the compiler report TRE0009, and have the builder never throw on depth.
findings.evidence:
Both parse sites use the default JsonDocument options, whose MaxDepth is 64. JsonTreeParser.cs:34 calls `JsonDocument.Parse(json)`. RuleBuilder.cs:792 calls `JsonDocument.Parse(this.ToJson())`. Neither reads CompilerOptions.MaxDepth. A grep of src/TruthWeaver for JsonDocumentOptions found it only in DecisionJsonReader, which is unrelated.

Parser exceptions: JsonTreeParser.cs:36 catches JsonException and returns a MalformedTree diagnostic. RuleBuilder.Compile (lines 780-794) has no try/catch around the Parse call, so a JsonException escapes. That breaks the "Compile never throws for authoring errors" rule in CLAUDE.md.

The writer side does not fail first. `ToNode().ToJsonString()` at RuleBuilder.cs:761 writes with the JsonWriter default depth of 1000, so it produces the over-deep text and the later Parse throws.

I did not run it. The depth arithmetic comes from the claim: each tree level takes two JSON levels (object plus operands array), plus args and array literals. By that count a 32-deep rule reaches about 65 levels. RuleNodeCompiler.cs:226 allows MaxDepth up to 32, and raising MaxDepth makes it worse.

Severity: I rate it medium, not high. A rule 32 levels deep is already past the DeepNesting lint threshold of 24 (0.75 times 32). The failure is a crash or misleading diagnostic only at the edge of the depth limit, and it affects only the JSON and builder paths. The builder's uncaught JsonException is still a real contract violation.

findings.title: Rendering a decision with any evaluated quantifier throws: trace shape does not match the outline
findings.summary: CompiledRule.OutlineOf gives a quantifier exactly one operand, its body (CompiledRule.Printing.cs:671). CollectionBinding gives the quantifier's TraceNode one child per element, each wrapping [body] (CollectionBinding.cs:206/221), and no children for an empty, null or faulted collection (lines 119/129/138). AssertOperandCountsAligned compares the two positionally and throws. Only the structural (no-trace) quantifier printing is tested (QuantifierFormsTests:151).
findings.failure_scenario: Evaluate `FORALL(x IN items, elementTrue)` with IncludeTrace over 0, 1 or 2 items, then call `rule.PrintMermaid(decision)`, PrintDot, PrintHtml or PrintPlainText(decision). Each throws InvalidOperationException 'OutlineNode/TraceNode operand-count mismatch', although the decision came from the same rule.
findings.expected_behavior: Make RuleRenderTree aware of quantifiers: map element children onto the body outline, or render per-element nodes. The evaluator trace and the printers must agree on shape.
findings.evidence:
I traced the mismatch in code but did not run it. The printer entry points that take a decision are the traced overloads in PlainTextTreePrinter.cs:46, MermaidTreePrinter.cs:112, HtmlPrinter.cs:34 and DotPrinter.cs:31. Each calls RuleRenderTree.Build(root, traceTree, ...). Build (RuleRenderTree.cs:56-65) calls AssertOperandCountsAligned first. That check (line 167) throws InvalidOperationException when a TraceNode is evaluated and its Children.Count differs from OutlineNode.Operands.Count.

Outline side: CompiledRule.Printing.cs:661-675 gives a QuantifierExpression exactly one operand, `[OutlineOf(quantifier.Body)]`.

Trace side: CollectionBinding.cs builds the quantifier's TraceNode differently.
- Lines 119, 129 and 138 handle a faulted, null or empty collection. They return a TraceNode with zero children, so 0 != 1 and the check throws.
- Lines 165, 183 and 206 add one child per element, labelled `x[i]`. Each wraps the body trace as a single child.
- With 2 or more elements the quantifier's child count is not 1, so the check throws at the quantifier node.
- With exactly 1 element the counts match at the quantifier node. The recursion then pairs the body outline with the `x[0]` element TraceNode. Build lines 75-79 do this positionally, with no quantifier-aware mapping. The body outline is a term with 0 operands, but the element node has 1 child (the body trace), so the check throws one level down.
- A short-circuited ForAll or Exists can leave the same shape mismatch.

I found no quantifier special-casing in RuleRenderTree.Build. So rendering any traced decision that includes an evaluated quantifier throws, for 0, 1 and 2 elements as claimed. Structural (no-trace) printing does not call the check, which fits the claim that only that path is tested.

Severity: it is a deterministic exception from a public API on a valid decision from the same rule, in a feature added by ADR-0010. It does not affect evaluation or semantics. It only breaks the trace renderers for quantifier rules, so I rate it high, and medium would be defensible.

findings.title: Invalid UTF-16 in JSON input throws ArgumentException instead of a diagnostic or a false result
findings.summary: JsonDocument.Parse(string) transcodes to UTF-8 and throws ArgumentException (wrapping EncoderFallbackException) for a lone surrogate. JsonTreeParser.Parse and DecisionJsonReader.TryRead (DecisionJsonReader.cs:40) catch only JsonException, against their 'never throws for malformed input' contracts. RuleBuilder string values with a lone surrogate also fail in ToJsonString.
findings.failure_scenario: `compiler.CompileJson("{\"predicate\":\"a\uD800\"}")` (a C# string holding an unpaired high surrogate, for example from truncated input) throws ArgumentException instead of returning MalformedTree. `DecisionRecord` reading via TryRead throws instead of returning false.
findings.expected_behavior: Catch ArgumentException from the transcode, or validate UTF-16 first, and report MalformedTree or return false with an error.

findings.title: RuleBuilder accepts double NaN/Infinity arguments, then Compile throws
findings.summary: UnsupportedValueType treats every double as supported, and ValueToNode (line 846) wraps it with JsonValue.Create. Utf8JsonWriter rejects NaN and Infinity, so ToJson(), called from Compile at line 792, throws ArgumentException. The builder documents that a value JSON cannot carry is an ArgumentTypeMismatch diagnostic from Compile.
findings.failure_scenario: `RuleBuilder.Predicate("scoreAbove", ("min", double.NaN)).Compile(compiler)` throws ArgumentException instead of returning a CompilationResult with TRE ArgumentTypeMismatch.
findings.expected_behavior: Report non-finite doubles in CollectProblems as ArgumentTypeMismatch.

findings.title: YAML duplicate-key rescan labels any repeat under a key named 'args' as DuplicateArgument
findings.summary: FindDuplicateArgument decides it is inside an args mapping with `top.Path.EndsWith(".args")`. A definition named `args`, or a predicate argument named `args` whose value is a variable-reference mapping, also has that path suffix.
findings.expected_behavior: Track that the frame is the 'args' member of a predicate node, not only the path text.

findings.title: A multi-document YAML stream silently compiles only the first document
findings.summary: Parse uses stream.Documents[0] and ignores the rest. The JSON surface rejects trailing content as malformed, so the two tree formats disagree on a stream with more than one document.
findings.failure_scenario:
`const: true
---
const: false
` compiles to True with no diagnostic. A reviewer who reads the whole file may take the second document as the rule.
findings.expected_behavior: Report MalformedTree when the stream holds more than one document.

findings.title: Quantifier trace label uses the registered collection name while the rule's canonical/trace text uses the name as written, so a case-different collection name breaks coverage pairing
findings.summary: `CollectionBinding.EvaluateQuantifierAsync` labels the quantifier's trace node and flat entries with the binding's registered `name` (`$"{label}({variable} IN {name})"`), but `RuleNodeCompiler.BuildQuantifier` (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:442) stores `node.CollectionName` exactly as the author wrote it, and `TraceText.Of` (TraceText.cs:29) and `CanonicalPrinter` print that written name. Collection lookup is case-insensitive (`PredicateRegistry.TryGetCollection` upper-cases the key), so the two texts differ whenever the rule spells the collection with different casing than the registration. `RuleCoverageAccumulator.Pair` (RuleCoverageAccumulator.cs:313) compares `traceNode.Text == this.texts[index]` for non-term nodes and throws `Mismatch` on any difference; the comment on TraceText.cs:25 says the two must match exactly. Terms do not have this problem because the compiler resolves a term to its schema's registered name. The same unnormalised name also makes `FORALL(x IN Lines, b)` and `FORALL(x IN lines, b)` two different analyzer atoms (ADR-0010 decision 8) even though they denote the same collection. The compiler side looks wrong: it should carry `binding.Name` into the `QuantifierExpression` (or the binding should use the written name), as it already does for predicates.
findings.failure_scenario: Register `AddCollection("lines", ...)`, compile `FORALL(line IN Lines, inStock)` (compiles cleanly), evaluate with `IncludeTrace`, then `new RuleCoverage(rule).Add(decision)`: the quantifier node's trace text is `FORALL(line IN lines)` while the rule's text is `FORALL(line IN Lines)`, so coverage throws `ArgumentException: The trace tree of the decision does not match the rule at '$'` for a decision of the very same rule.
findings.expected_behavior: Per ADR-0010 decision 7 and docs/strong-k3/quantifiers/*.md, coverage folds element children onto the body node for any decision of the rule; the trace label and the rule text for a quantifier must be identical regardless of how the author cased the collection name, exactly as a term's label is the registered predicate name.
findings.evidence:
I traced the path through the code and did not run it.

1. Lookup is case-insensitive. `PredicateRegistry.TryGetCollection` (PredicateRegistry.cs:84-87) upper-cases the key. `RuleNodeCompiler.BuildQuantifier` (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:372, 442) resolves the binding, then builds `new QuantifierExpression(node.Kind, node.Variable, node.CollectionName, bodyTree)`. `node.CollectionName` is the text as written, and nothing in the compiler replaces it with `binding.Name`. So `FORALL(line IN Lines, ...)` compiles cleanly against a collection registered as `lines`.

2. The rule's text uses the written name. `TraceText.Of` (TraceText.cs:29) prints `{label}({q.Variable} IN {q.CollectionName})`. `CanonicalPrinter` (CanonicalPrinter.cs:276) does the same. `Evaluator.EvalQuantifierAsync` (Evaluator.cs:432) builds its description from `node.CollectionName` too, but only uses it on the defensive unregistered-collection branch.

3. The runtime trace uses the registered name. On the normal path, `Evaluator.cs:448-464` calls `binding.EvaluateQuantifierAsync` and returns that `TraceNode` unchanged. `CollectionBinding.cs:72` builds `description = $"{label}({variable} IN {name})"`, where `name` is the registered name. That string is the root `TraceNode` text, at lines 119, 129, 138 and 221, and the flat `TraceEntry`, at line 77.

4. Coverage compares the two texts. `RuleCoverageAccumulator.Pair` (RuleCoverageAccumulator.cs:311-317) compares non-term nodes with `traceNode.Text == this.texts[index]` and throws `Mismatch` on any difference. The quantifier node is not a `TermExpression`, so it takes the strict equality branch. With `lines` registered and `Lines` written, the trace text is `FORALL(line IN lines)` and the rule text is `FORALL(line IN Lines)`. `RuleCoverage.Add` then throws `ArgumentException` for a decision of the same rule.

The trigger needs a trace-bearing decision, a `RuleCoverage` consumer, and a collection name whose casing differs from its registration. Quantifiers written with exactly the registered casing are unaffected.

I did not trace the secondary claim that `Lines` and `lines` become two separate analyzer atoms. It is plausible, because the expression stores the name unnormalised.

Severity: a real crash in a documented feature, but it needs a casing mismatch, and the fix is small. The trace text, the flat entries and the memo keys all have to switch to the same name. I rate it medium rather than high.

findings.title: ANY/ALL/NONE pages say the params RuleBuilder overload rejects fewer than two operands; the code folds them
findings.summary: any.md:496, all.md:287 and none.md:2232 (Edge cases) state 'Only `RuleBuilder.Any(IEnumerable<RuleBuilder>)` applies a convention, at build time ... `RuleBuilder.Any(params RuleBuilder[])` rejects fewer than two operands like the rule languages.' `RuleBuilder.Any(params RuleBuilder[])` (RuleBuilder.cs:353-363), `All` (387-397) and `None` (421-431) fold exactly as the sequence overload does: empty becomes a constant, one operand becomes itself (or `NOT` for `NONE`), and the XML remarks say this is deliberate so array and list give the same rule. The documentation is the side that is wrong (the Syntax table on the same pages, 'for two or more operands', is also misleading).
findings.failure_scenario: A library consumer reads any.md, calls `RuleBuilder.Any(single)` expecting a compile diagnostic (`InfixArityViolation`) that would catch an accidental one-element array, and instead gets a rule that silently compiles to `single`; `RuleBuilder.Any()` with no operands compiles to the constant `False` instead of failing.
findings.expected_behavior: The reference pages describe the package as it behaves: both `Any`/`All`/`None` overloads fold an empty or single-operand list (identity constant, the operand, or `NOT` operand), and only the rule languages reject fewer than two operands.

findings.title: GreaterThan and LessThan pages claim there is no IEnumerable RuleBuilder overload; both overloads exist
findings.summary: greaterthan.md (Syntax table and the sentence after it, 'RuleBuilder has only the params overload for GreaterThan; there is no IEnumerable overload') and lessthan.md make the same claim for `LessThan`. `RuleBuilder.GreaterThan(int k, IEnumerable<RuleBuilder>)` (RuleBuilder.cs:642) and `RuleBuilder.LessThan(int k, IEnumerable<RuleBuilder>)` (RuleBuilder.cs:663) exist and are tested (`RuleBuilderOverloadConsistencyTests.GreaterThanAndLessThan_WithAList_BuildTheSameRuleAsTheArray_Test`). ADR-0005 log row 43 only lists `Between`, `AtLeast`, `AtMost`, `Exactly`, so the doc text was written from the ADR rather than the code. The documentation is the wrong side.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer with a runtime-length list writes `RuleBuilder.GreaterThan(1, list.ToArray())` or avoids the operator because the page says the overload does not exist; the public API surface is misdescribed.
findings.expected_behavior: The pages list `RuleBuilder.GreaterThan(int k, IEnumerable<RuleBuilder>)` and `RuleBuilder.LessThan(int k, IEnumerable<RuleBuilder>)` with the same 'not folded' note the AtLeast/AtMost/Exactly pages carry.

findings.title: ADR-0005 decisions 13/14 name MalformedTree for too-few ANY/ALL/NONE/BETWEEN operands and non-integer BETWEEN bounds; docs and code use InfixArityViolation and InvalidThresholdValue
findings.summary: ADR-0005 lines 418-420 and 439 say fewer than two operands for `ANY`/`ALL`/`NONE`/`BETWEEN` 'is `MalformedTree`', and lines 445-446 say non-integer `min`/`max` in JSON/YAML are 'else `MalformedTree`'. The compiler raises `InfixArityViolation` (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:458 via BuildVariadic, :659 for BETWEEN) and the tree reader raises `InvalidThresholdValue` for a missing or non-integer bound (TreeFormatReader.cs:561); docs/strong-k3/cardinality/any.md:491, between.md:1150-1153 and specification/diagnostics.md:22 agree with the code. The ADR is the stale side; the task frames an ADR as ground truth, so it should be amended in place (as ADR-0005 already is elsewhere) rather than left contradicting the reference.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader checking `{"op":"between","min":1.5,"max":2,"operands":[...]}` against the ADR expects `TRE0014` (MalformedTree) and writes tooling or tests around that code; the engine reports `TRE0008` (InvalidThresholdValue).
findings.expected_behavior: ADR-0005's implemented-in notes for k3-conformance 13 and 14 name `InfixArityViolation` (`TRE0006`) for the operand minimum and `InvalidThresholdValue` (`TRE0008`) for a missing or non-integer bound, matching diagnostics.md and the code.

findings.title: BETWEEN and NONE pages say Simplify keeps the node; Simplify rewrites either one when an operand is a constant
findings.summary: between.md:1171 says '`Simplify` and `Canonicalize` keep `BETWEEN`' and none.md:2190/2244 say the same for `NONE`. `Simplifier.Rewrite` (Simplifier.cs:371-372) sends `AnyExpression or AllExpression or NoneExpression or ExactlyOneExpression or BetweenExpression` to `ViaExpansion`, which, whenever any operand is a `ConstantExpression`, expands the node one level (`PrimitiveExpander.ExpandTop`) and keeps the simplified result if it is no larger. The sentence is true only for the no-constant case; the docs are the imprecise side (ADR-0005 decision 10, k3-conformance 27, explicitly lists 'any other derived operator with a constant operand expanded one level').
findings.failure_scenario: `BETWEEN(1, 2, True, a, b)` simplifies to `AtMost(1, a, b)` (AtLeast side folds to True after the shift), and `NONE(True, a)` simplifies to the constant `False`; a reader relying on the page's 'keeps BETWEEN/NONE' round-trip expectation sees a different node kind after `Simplify()`.
findings.expected_behavior: The pages state that `Simplify` keeps `BETWEEN`/`NONE` unless an operand is a constant, in which case the derived-with-constant rule may expand it to thresholds or fold it, as ADR-0005 decision 10 describes.

findings.title: DSL reads a definition parameter named T, F or U as a constant; JSON/YAML/builder read it as the parameter
findings.summary: ParsePrimary checks the letter constants T/F/U (lines 569-585) before it checks the current definition's parameters (line 688), and ExpectParameterName (799-804) accepts any identifier, so a parameter spelled t, f or u is silently compiled as True/False/Unknown and the use's argument is discarded. TreeFormatReader.ReadNodeCore (237-247) and RuleBuilder.Define take the predicate branch first, so the same document in JSON, YAML or the builder expands the parameter correctly. ADR-0008 decision 4 requires the four forms to give an identical tree, and ADR-0008 decision 6 lists T/F/U only for definition names, not parameters.
findings.failure_scenario: Rule text `let pick(c, t, f) = c ? t : f; pick(isAdmin, canEdit, canView)` compiles with no diagnostic to `If(isAdmin, True, False)`: with isAdmin True and canEdit False the result is True instead of False. The JSON form `{"definitions":{"pick":{"parameters":["c","t","f"],"body":{"op":"if","operands":[{"predicate":"c"},{"predicate":"t"},{"predicate":"f"}]}}},"op":"use","name":"pick","operands":[...]}` compiles to `If(isAdmin, canEdit, canView)`, so the two formats disagree. The code side is wrong: parameter names need the same reserved-word/letter guard as definition names (or the parameter check must precede the constant check).
findings.expected_behavior: A parameter named T, F or U is either rejected with DefinitionNameCollision-style diagnostic in every format, or is read as the parameter in rule text exactly as JSON, YAML and RuleBuilder read it, so the compiled tree is identical across formats.
findings.evidence: Traced in src/TruthWeaver/Parsing/DslParser.cs. ExpectParameterName (799-804) accepts any Identifier, so `let pick(c, t, f) = ...` declares parameters t and f. Line 790 puts them in currentParameters, case-insensitively. In ParsePrimary, the T/F/U check (569-585) runs when the identifier is not followed by '('. IsKeyword is the same case-insensitive check used for the other keywords. In the body `c ? t : f`, `t` is followed by ':' and `f` by ';', so each returns ConsumeConstant at 573-583 and ParsePrimary returns early. The parameter-reference branch (688-698) is never reached, so the parameter becomes a constant and the use's argument is dropped. DefinitionExpander.cs:45 applies the reserved-word check (DslParser.IsReservedWord, ReservedWords.cs includes "T") to definition names only. No parameter name is checked for reserved words in the expander, so no DefinitionNameCollision or other diagnostic appears. I did not re-read TreeFormatReader or RuleBuilder. The cross-format divergence rests on the claim. The DSL half is traced in full: it gives a silent wrong tree, `If(isAdmin, True, False)`. Severity is high rather than critical. The trigger needs a parameter literally named t, f or u, which is plausible for ternary-style definitions. The failure is a silent wrong decision, but it is limited to the DSL and has a simple workaround of renaming the parameter.

findings.title: A duplicate parameter name in one definition is accepted and silently drops an argument
findings.summary: ExpandUse binds parameters into a case-insensitive dictionary by name, so `let f(x, x) = ...` (accepted by DslParser.ExpectParameterName, TreeFormatReader.ReadDefinitionEntry and RuleBuilder.Define without a check) binds only the last argument and the earlier one is discarded with no diagnostic. The term-argument precedent (DuplicateArgument, TRE0032, 'no occurrence wins') rejects the same mistake for predicate arguments.
findings.failure_scenario: `let both(x, X) = x AND X; both(isOwner, isEditor)` compiles without a diagnostic to `isEditor AND isEditor`; with isOwner False and isEditor True the rule yields True instead of False.
findings.expected_behavior: A definition whose parameter list repeats a name (case-insensitively) is a compile error in every format, in the same family as DuplicateArgument.

findings.title: A note written on a `use` node is dropped when the use expands
findings.summary: ExpandUse returns ExpandNode(definition.Body, ...) and never carries the UseNode's own Note onto the expanded root (Carry is applied only to the body's nodes), so the note is lost before NoteCollector runs. rule-tree.schema.json lists `note` on useNode, rule-formats.md:209 says any JSON node can have one and rule-formats.md:16 promises `parse(print(x))` keeps the same notes; a use whose body root has no note of its own loses the annotation with no diagnostic.
findings.failure_scenario: JSON `{"definitions":{"adult":{"body":{"predicate":"isAdult"}}},"op":"use","name":"adult","note":"age gate"}` (or rule text `let adult = isAdult; /* age gate */ adult`) compiles, but CompiledRule.Notes is empty and PrintJson()/PrintRuleText() of the compiled rule no longer contain 'age gate'. The code side is wrong: the use's note should land on the expanded root (or the loss should be documented and the key rejected).
findings.expected_behavior: A note on a use node is kept on the node the use expands to (or joined with that node's own note), so CompiledRule.Notes and the printers preserve it.

findings.title: coalesce.md says RuleBuilder.Coalesce(IEnumerable) folds an empty or single list; the code, rulebuilder.md and the pinned test say it does not
findings.summary: The reference page states 'an empty list builds the constant Unknown and a single operand builds that operand unchanged', but RuleBuilder.Coalesce(IEnumerable) (RuleBuilder.cs:487-498) builds the unfolded node and its remark says 'A short or empty sequence is not folded, because COALESCE has no identity constant'; docs/rulebuilder.md:54 and RuleBuilderEnumerableTests pin the no-fold behavior. The two reference pages contradict each other, and the code's stated reason is false: coalesce.md:65 and :145-155 correctly say Unknown is COALESCE's identity on both sides, so folding would be K3-sound.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller who follows coalesce.md writes `RuleBuilder.Coalesce(checks)` with an empty `checks` list expecting the constant Unknown; the builder instead renders `{"op":"coalesce","operands":[]}` and Compile returns InfixArityViolation (TRE0006), so the rule fails to compile. The strong-k3 page is the side that disagrees with the pinned behavior; whichever side the owner keeps, the other page and the code remark must change.
findings.expected_behavior: coalesce.md, rulebuilder.md and RuleBuilder.Coalesce(IEnumerable) describe one behavior; if no-fold is kept, the reason given should not claim COALESCE lacks an identity.

findings.title: rule-text.md and ADR-0005 say JSON/YAML do not read the constant letters, but the readers, the schema and syntax.md accept them
findings.summary: rule-text.md:204 ('JSON and YAML read the words only') and ADR-0005 decision 16 ('JSON and YAML do not read the letters') contradict JsonNodeCursor.TryGetTruthValue (JsonNodeCursor.cs:112) and YamlNodeCursor.TryGetTruthValue (YamlNodeCursor.cs:112), which accept T/F/U via TruthValueText.TryParseLetter, and contradict rule-tree.schema.json:61-69 and docs/strong-k3/specification/syntax.md:16, which document the letters as accepted. Code, schema and the K3 reference agree; rule-text.md and the ADR are the wrong side.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader of rule-text.md expects `{"const": "U"}` to be a MalformedTree error and relies on that to catch a typo; the compiler accepts it as Unknown. Conversely a validator written from rule-text.md rejects documents the compiler accepts.
findings.expected_behavior: rule-text.md (and the ADR amendment) state that JSON and YAML read the words and the letters T, F and U, matching the schema and syntax.md.

findings.title: ADR-0005 says a wrong operand count for If and the inspections is MalformedTree; the code and the K3 reference report InfixArityViolation
findings.summary: Decision 13 (k3-conformance 16, line 491; k3-conformance 17, line 510) and the 'Decided, If (log row 19)' entry (line 664) say the operand-count error is MalformedTree. RuleNodeCompiler.BuildIf (RuleNodeCompiler.cs:325) and BuildInspection (:351) report InfixArityViolation (TRE0006), and docs/strong-k3/functions/if.md:26, istrue.md:29 and diagnostics.md's TRE0006 row document that code. The ADR is stale relative to the shipped behavior and the reference pages.
findings.failure_scenario: A host that follows the ADR filters compile results for TRE0014 to detect `If(a, b)` written in JSON; the compiler emits TRE0006 instead and the mistake is not caught by that filter.
findings.expected_behavior: ADR-0005 carries an in-place amendment that the If/inspection arity error is InfixArityViolation (TRE0006), as the reference documents.

findings.title: ADR-0005 decision 12 documents Decision.Project(bool unknownAs); the API and project.md use a TruthValue parameter
findings.summary: Decision 12 (lines 334-337) and decision 19 (line 626) say `Decision.Project(bool unknownAs)` with the rationale that a bool makes an Unknown replacement unrequestable. Decision.cs:82 declares `Project(TruthValue unknownAs)` and throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for Unknown; docs/strong-k3/result-transformations/project.md:11 and :27 document the TruthValue form. Code and reference agree; the ADR is stale.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller following the ADR writes `decision.Project(false)`; it does not compile (no implicit bool to TruthValue conversion).
findings.expected_behavior: ADR-0005 decisions 12 and 19 are amended in place to the TruthValue signature and the throw-on-Unknown rule.

findings.title: rewriting-rules.md and NormalForms.cs call `If` not information-monotone, contradicting the K3 reference
findings.summary: docs/rewriting-rules.md:320 ('COALESCE, the inspections ... and If are not information-monotone, so each is an atom') and :375, and the comment at NormalForms.cs:268, classify If as non-monotone. docs/strong-k3/functions/if.md:16 and docs/strong-k3/specification/semantics.md:184 state If is a Strong Kleene connective, monotone in the information order. Keeping If as an NNF atom is a sound design choice, but the stated reason is false and contradicts the reference.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader of rewriting-rules.md concludes a rule containing If is outside the no-tautology theorem and NAND/NOR expressiveness, which semantics.md says applies only to COALESCE and the inspections; ExpandToNand actually does expand If fully.
findings.expected_behavior: rewriting-rules.md and the NormalForms.cs comment give the real reason If stays an atom in NNF (a design choice to keep the node) and do not call it non-monotone.
